title: Hot Fuzz
logline: A London supercop is transferred to a sleepy village. Dense setup-and-payoff action-movie parody.
overview: Former London constable Nicholas Angel finds it difficult to adapt to his new assignment in the sleepy British village of Sandford. Not only does he miss the excitement of the big city, but he also has a well-meaning oaf for a partner. However, when a series of grisly accidents rocks Sandford, Angel smells something rotten in the idyllic village.
tagline: Big cops. Small town. Moderate violence.

jokes.text: Most recently in December when wounded by a man dressed as Father Christmas.
jokes.setup: A rapid-fire montage of Nicholas Angel's impressive CV — bravery awards, commendations, elite training — delivered in a dry bureaucratic voiceover tone.
jokes.punchline: The final injury detail undercuts the heroic summary with an absurdly festive attacker, delivered in the same flat tone as 'Received the Baton of Honor.'
jokes.explanation: Edgar Wright weaponizes the CV montage format: escalating accomplishments set up an expectation of heroic grandeur, then the punchline is maximally deflating — the last injury listed is from a Father Christmas. The deadpan delivery makes it land harder. It's a structurally near-perfect cold-open gag: the entire opening exists to build to this. Earns a high craft score for precision economy and structural elegance.

jokes.text: Your arrest record is 400% higher than any other officer — which is why it's high time that such skills were put to better use. We're making you Sergeant. In Sandford, Gloucestershire.
jokes.setup: Angel is being praised in lavish terms for his exceptional arrest record and performance; the audience expects a promotion within London.
jokes.punchline: His reward for excellence is exile to a rural backwater — the institutional logic is that he's too good and must be removed.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection: 'skills put to better use' implies a prestigious posting, the punchline is Sandford. The joke also efficiently establishes the film's core premise in a single beat. The geographical specificity ('Gloucestershire') adds to the comedy.

jokes.text: That's in the country. / Yes, lovely.
jokes.setup: Angel is reeling from learning his new posting is in rural Gloucestershire.
jokes.punchline: His superior's breezy 'Yes, lovely' is a perfect non-answer that treats his protest as if it were enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: A compact, clean bit of British understatement comedy. 'Lovely' deployed against Angel's horror is a good word choice that doubles down on the institutional indifference. Brief but effective.

jokes.text: No. / No. / No. — the triple refusal sequence
jokes.setup: Angel tries every available option: stay as Sergeant, stay as a PC, have any choice at all.
jokes.punchline: Three consecutive flat 'No's demolish each escape route in rapid succession, the rhythm itself becoming the joke.
jokes.explanation: Edgar Wright's signature use of rhythmic cutting and repetition; three options, three monosyllabic negations, escalating Angel's helplessness. The structure carries the comedy more than the content. Economy score is high because it achieves a lot with almost nothing.

jokes.text: Well, you've always wanted to transfer to the country. / In 20 years or so, yes. / Well done, you.
jokes.setup: The superior invokes Angel's own expressed desire to move to the country as justification.
jokes.punchline: 'Well done, you' — delivered as insincere congratulation for being transferred 20 years too early, treating Angel's objection as confirmation.
jokes.explanation: 'Well done, you' is an exquisitely British piece of condescension — sarcastic congratulation that refuses to engage with the actual complaint. Good economy and character work from the superior.

jokes.text: Hello, Nicholas. How's the hand? / It's still a bit stiff. — the Inspector repeats the identical greeting
jokes.setup: Angel was already greeted by his sergeant with 'Hello, Nicholas, how's the hand?' and answered identically. Now he's escalated to the Inspector.
jokes.punchline: The Inspector opens with the exact same words, suggesting the whole organisation uses the same script — the gag is the system's uniformity, not any individual.
jokes.explanation: Hot Fuzz's signature joke structure: exact repetition as comedic escalation. The first occurrence was normal; the second reveals the whole institution is a closed loop. It pays off again with the Chief Inspector. Brilliant economy — the same five words do three times the work.

jokes.text: He's staying at the Section House, sir. With the recruits. / Yes, he's living out of cardboard boxes. / Well, then, you're packed already.
jokes.setup: The Inspector asks where Angel is living, ostensibly out of concern.
jokes.punchline: 'Well, then, you're packed already' — the pathetic detail of living out of boxes is instantly weaponised as a reason to expedite his transfer, turning pity into bureaucratic efficiency.
jokes.explanation: Sharp joke that doubles as character revelation: the superior's feigned sympathy is immediately converted into an argument against Angel. The punchline has genuine wit — it's logical and cruel simultaneously.

jokes.text: No, I'm sorry. I'm gonna have to... / You want to take this higher? / Yes, yes, I do. / You want me to bother the Chief Inspector with this? / Yes. / You want me to get the Chief Inspector to come all the way down here? / Yes, I do. / Okay. Kenneth!
jokes.setup: The Inspector uses a series of increasingly incredulous questions to dissuade Angel from escalating — building the Chief Inspector up as a distant, unreachable authority.
jokes.punchline: 'Kenneth!' — shouted immediately, revealing the Chief Inspector is literally next door; all the buildup was hollow bluster.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best constructed jokes. Three escalating rhetorical questions build an enormous edifice of institutional gravity, then 'Kenneth!' demolishes it in one syllable. The punchline's power comes entirely from the structure that precedes it — this is textbook comedy construction. High earned-vs-cheap because the payoff rewards patience.

jokes.text: Hello, Nicholas. How's the hand? — the Chief Inspector repeats the same greeting a third time
jokes.setup: Angel has now heard this exact greeting from his Sergeant and his Inspector.
jokes.punchline: The Chief Inspector — the supposedly remote authority — opens with the identical words, completing the trilogy and confirming the entire Met is a single hive mind.
jokes.explanation: The rule-of-three completion is perfectly executed. The first was setup, the second established the pattern, the third — coming immediately after the 'Kenneth!' joke — delivers the most satisfying payoff. The comic logic is airtight: the more prestigious the official, the more they're revealed to be interchangeable automatons. This earns 8+ because it's the culmination of a carefully built multi-beat structure that also reveals something true about bureaucratic institutions.

jokes.text: You've been rather letting the side down... You'll continue to be exceptional and we can't have that. You'll put us all out of a job.
jokes.setup: Angel expects to be praised or at least given a rational bureaucratic reason for his transfer.
jokes.punchline: The stated reason is that he's too good — his competence is itself the problem, delivered with utter sincerity by the Chief Inspector.
jokes.explanation: A solid satirical joke about institutional mediocrity: excellence is punished because it exposes everyone else. The idea is familiar but executed with good specificity ('you'll continue to be exceptional and we can't have that').

jokes.text: You can't just make people disappear. / Yes, I can. I'm the Chief Inspector.
jokes.setup: Angel makes a principled objection: institutions cannot simply vanish individuals against their will.
jokes.punchline: The Chief Inspector corrects him with complete sincerity — the job title IS the justification.
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. The punchline works on two levels: it's funny as a straight power-abuse joke, and it foreshadows the film's themes about authority without oversight. The deadpan delivery of 'I'm the Chief Inspector' as complete logical justification is the joke's engine. High quotability.

jokes.text: There's one thing you haven't taken into account — what the 'team' is gonna make of this. [Cut to: Angel alone, colleagues apparently indifferent]
jokes.setup: Angel invokes his team as a final trump card — implying they will rally to his defense.
jokes.punchline: The implied visual: his colleagues are entirely unbothered or actively pleased to see him go, completely undermining his argument.
jokes.explanation: The 17-second gap [05:01–05:18] before the phone scene suggests a visual beat showing the team's indifference. The joke is in the gap between Angel's confidence and reality. Functional and character-revealing.

jokes.text: What's the situation? / You know the situation. We've been over this. / No, I… I meant here. / Two people involved, distinct signs of a struggle. Complete mess.
jokes.setup: Angel shows up outside what appears to be a crime scene and asks 'what's the situation' — a professional police inquiry.
jokes.punchline: Janine thinks he's asking about their relationship; Angel clarifies he meant the physical scene; Janine's crime-scene description ('two people involved, distinct signs of a struggle') applies perfectly to both.
jokes.explanation: Clever double-meaning joke that works on multiple levels simultaneously: it's a linguistic misunderstanding joke, a character joke (Angel defaults to police speak), AND it uses Janine's crime-scene language to describe their breakup ('two people involved, distinct signs of a struggle, complete mess'), which is both funny and emotionally resonant. The dual meaning is entirely earned, not a stretch. This is excellent craft — earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Janine, I've been transferred. I'm moving away for a while. / I'm not Janine.
jokes.setup: Angel delivers his prepared speech to who he thinks is Janine.
jokes.punchline: He's been talking to the wrong person — an immediately deflating reveal.
jokes.explanation: Classic mistaken-identity beat. The gag works efficiently enough — he delivers the speech twice — but it's a fairly standard comedic device. The payoff of delivering the speech again is the better joke.

jokes.text: Janine, I've been transferred. I'm moving away for a while. / I know. Bob told me.
jokes.setup: Having just told the wrong person, Angel re-delivers his prepared speech to the actual Janine, expecting it to land as news.
jokes.punchline: She already knows, via Bob — his careful plan to tell her 'in person' is completely deflated.
jokes.explanation: The double deflation (wrong person, then already-knows) compounds the embarrassment effectively. Each beat individually is modest but together they form a good cringe sequence.

jokes.text: You were already married to the force, weren't you? / We're actually supposed to call it 'the service' now. Official vocab guidelines state that 'force' is too aggressive.
jokes.setup: Janine delivers an emotional accusation — 'you were already married to the force' — a classic relationship complaint.
jokes.punchline: Angel corrects the terminology with bureaucratic precision, entirely missing the emotional point, which proves Janine's point perfectly.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. It's simultaneously a character joke (Angel cannot switch off), a structural joke (the correction IS the proof of the accusation), and a satirical joke about institutional language policing. The punchline is perfect: 'Official vocab guidelines state that force is too aggressive' is a brilliantly specific detail that could only come from this character. It's also devastating for the relationship — by correcting her, he proves every word she just said. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor; this exceeds it slightly because of how much it does at once.

jokes.text: No, you're right, you do have that rubber plant.
jokes.setup: Angel protests that it's not 'all he cares about' — defending himself from the accusation of emotional unavailability.
jokes.punchline: Janine sarcastically concedes: yes, there IS one other thing — a rubber plant. The bathos is total.
jokes.explanation: Superb economy — 'that rubber plant' is an inspired specific detail. The bathos of offering a houseplant as evidence of emotional depth is perfectly chosen. It's also a setup for joke 18.

jokes.text: It's a Japanese Peace Lily.
jokes.setup: Janine dismissively calls it 'that rubber plant'.
jokes.punchline: Angel corrects the plant species with the same hair-trigger precision he used to correct 'force' vs 'service' — proving again he cannot let inaccuracy pass even in an emotional conversation.
jokes.explanation: Four words do enormous work. It's a callback to the 'force/service' correction, confirming this is a character trait not an isolated incident. The plant species is perfectly chosen — 'Japanese Peace Lily' is specific, slightly exotic, and the word 'Peace' is ironic in the middle of a breakup argument. Character integration is nearly perfect: only Angel would do this, only here would it be this funny. Earns high craft score.

jokes.text: Actually, there's something I need to tell you. / You're seeing someone else. / Yes. How did you... / Is it Bob? / No. / Does Bob look like the kind of person I'd go out with? / It's Dave. / Hello, there.
jokes.setup: Janine wants to confess she's seeing someone; Angel correctly guesses immediately.
jokes.punchline: He guesses Bob first — implying 'Bob' is a plausible candidate which is apparently offensive to Janine; then 'It's Dave' followed immediately by Dave announcing himself.
jokes.explanation: The 'Hello, there' from Dave appearing right on cue is a good timing joke. Angel guessing correctly also shows his detective instincts extending into personal life — consistent with his character.

jokes.text: Oh, Nicholas. / You do realize that window was broken from the inside?
jokes.setup: An emotional moment — Janine says 'Oh, Nicholas' with sympathy/exasperation as the scene seems to be wrapping up with some feeling.
jokes.punchline: Angel immediately pivots to a forensic observation about the window, completely unable to leave detective mode even at the most human moment.
jokes.explanation: Perfect scene-closer. The emotional beats of the scene are carefully built so that 'Oh, Nicholas' feels like genuine closure — then the rug pull is a forensic observation that serves no emotional purpose whatsoever. It's the best possible encapsulation of Angel's character defect and pays off everything Janine just said about him. Earns 8+ for character integration and structural elegance as a scene-ender.

jokes.text: Nicholas, Frank again. One other thing about your cottage. It's not ready.
jokes.setup: A warm, jolly voicemail from Inspector Butterman offering Angel a lovely cottage — delivered in an almost comically enthusiastic tone.
jokes.punchline: Second message: the cottage isn't ready. The cheerfulness of the delivery against the uselessness of the news is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A quick situational gag — Angel's new posting is already going wrong before he arrives. The cheerfulness of 'Cheerio' followed by 'it's not ready' is a small but functional beat.

jokes.text: It would appear the heavens have opened.
jokes.setup: Angel arrives in Sandford in torrential rain — a classic 'pathetic fallacy' moment for his miserable reassignment.
jokes.punchline: He narrates it in the most formal, detached police-report language possible. 'It would appear the heavens have opened' as a description of getting absolutely soaked.
jokes.explanation: A great character-voice joke. 'It would appear the heavens have opened' is exactly how Angel would describe rain — formal, observational, evidence-based. The gap between the officialese and the physical reality (he's standing in a downpour) is perfectly chosen. High character integration.

jokes.text: But you've always been here. / Excuse me? / Oh, I'm sorry. I thought you were my husband.
jokes.setup: Angel enters the inn and says 'I was hoping to check in.' The innkeeper appears confused.
jokes.punchline: She thought he was her husband — she was talking to him as if he'd been gone forever. The confusion is played as matter-of-fact.
jokes.explanation: A quick mistaken-identity gag that also sketches the village's eccentricity. Functional but not exceptional — the joke mostly works as texture.

jokes.text: I trust you had a pleasant trip. Fascist. / I beg your pardon? / 'System of Government characterized by extreme dictatorship.' Seven across.
jokes.setup: Joyce makes welcoming small talk and then appears to call Angel a fascist — a shocking non-sequitur.
jokes.punchline: She's doing a crossword puzzle. 'Fascist' is the answer to seven across, delivered mid-sentence.
jokes.explanation: A clever structural gag that plays with the misdirection of conversational implication — 'Fascist' landing as an apparent insult before the clarification lands. The addition of her defining it ('System of Government characterized by extreme dictatorship') extends the joke with a deadpan definition. Good construction.

jokes.text: Well, actually, I could probably make my own way up. Hag. / I beg your pardon? / 'Evil old woman considered frightful or ugly.' It's 12 down.
jokes.setup: Established that Joyce reads crossword answers aloud mid-conversation, which made 'Fascist' sound like an insult to Angel.
jokes.punchline: Now Angel appears to call her a 'Hag' — the same joke structure reversed, with Angel in the position of saying the word. The running gag kicks in.
jokes.explanation: The second beat of the crossword running gag. While the structure is identical to the first, it works because the roles are reversed — now it's Angel who seems to be issuing the insult. Slightly less surprising than the first but still delivers. The running gag format is well-deployed.

jokes.text: They listed her age as 55. / When I'm actually 53. / Fifty-three.
jokes.setup: Roy explains why they don't like the local paper.
jokes.punchline: Roy's reason is that it misreported Mary's age; both say the number 53 with equal gravity, suggesting this minor inaccuracy is a profound grievance.
jokes.explanation: A compact sketch of small-town grievance politics — the local paper is resented for a two-year age error. Roy echoing '53' sells it. Good village character texture.

jokes.text: When's your birthday? / Twenty-second of February. / What year? / Every year. / Get out.
jokes.setup: Angel suspects the patron is underage and asks their birthday to calculate their age.
jokes.punchline: 'Every year' — the classic deflecting non-answer to 'what year were you born.' Angel's instant 'Get out' is the perfect no-nonsense response.
jokes.explanation: The 'every year' dodge is a known joke format but the rapid-fire execution and Angel's immediate 'Get out' gives it crisp timing. The escalation across three successive underage patrons works well.

jokes.text: When's your birthday? / Eighth of May, 1969. / You're 37? / Yeah. / Get out.
jokes.setup: Second underage patron; this one provides a full date of birth — apparently complying with Angel's request.
jokes.punchline: He's 37. He's not underage at all — Angel still kicks him out, presumably for being annoying or the wrong vibe. The escalation of the 'Get out' gag.
jokes.explanation: The twist that the 37-year-old also gets ejected takes the gag somewhere unexpected. The logic is that Angel is ejecting people on pure instinct now, or that the 37-year-old looks so rough he's still suspicious. Either reading is funny. Good escalation.

jokes.text: When's your birthday? / Out.
jokes.setup: Third round of the birthday ejection sequence.
jokes.punchline: Angel doesn't even wait for the answer — just 'Out.' The sequence has escalated to the point where he's ejecting on sight.
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation terminus. The structure is: full question-answer-ejection / question-wrong answer-ejection / question-no answer-ejection. Each beat strips away more of the transaction until it's down to 'Out.' This is Wright's comedic escalation method in miniature and the final beat has near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: Well, a few of them may be a month or two south of proper. But if they're in here, it stops them getting into trouble out there. Yeah, the way we see it, it's all for the greater good.
jokes.setup: Angel confronts Roy about the underage drinkers.
jokes.punchline: 'A month or two south of proper' is a magnificent evasive euphemism; the 'greater good' logic is both satirically true-to-life and the film's first use of its key catchphrase.
jokes.explanation: 'A month or two south of proper' is the film's funniest euphemism this early on — it's the kind of English understatement that covers a multitude of sins. The 'greater good' introduction here plants the seed for one of the film's major running gags, giving this joke significant rewatch value.

jokes.text: The greater good. / The greater good.
jokes.setup: Roy has just invoked 'the greater good' to justify the underage drinking.
jokes.punchline: Mary immediately echoes it, in unison or just after — the phrase is revealed as a village mantra rather than a personal conviction.
jokes.explanation: The echo transforms 'greater good' from a personal opinion into a collective ideology. This is the film's first hint of the village hive-mind that will become central to the plot. High rewatch value because on second viewing you clock this as sinister. The economy of a simple repeated phrase doing this much work is very good.

jokes.text: I hope you're not planning on driving that. / No. [long beat]
jokes.setup: Angel encounters a clearly drunk Danny sitting with or near a vehicle.
jokes.punchline: Danny's flat 'No' and the beat that follows — he's sitting there drunk but technically not driving. The comedic beat is the gap between Angel's inference and Danny's minimal compliance.
jokes.explanation: A quiet beat that sets up Danny's introduction; the humour is in Danny's minimal compliance and Angel's dawning realisation he's dealing with a cop.

jokes.text: Right. I'm taking you to the station. [23 second pause] Where is it?
jokes.setup: Angel delivers the authoritative 'I'm taking you to the station' line with full professional confidence.
jokes.punchline: He doesn't know where the station is. His authority immediately deflates.
jokes.explanation: The long pause before 'Where is it?' is essential — that beat is funnier than the words. Angel's confident professionalism punctured by the most basic logistical failure. Nicely timed.

jokes.text: 'Nicholas Angel.' / Oh, when did you start? / Tomorrow.
jokes.setup: Angel has apparently arrived at the station and is being processed or checked in.
jokes.punchline: He's reading his own name from the duty roster; the officer points out he doesn't start until tomorrow. Angel has arrested a village full of people on his day off.
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Angel cannot not police. He's arrested a large number of people before his first official day. The implication that he launched a pub operation on his day off is entirely consistent with everything we've learned about him.

jokes.text: Well, I see you've already arrested the whole village.
jokes.setup: Angel has apparently brought in a large number of people from the pub.
jokes.punchline: The officer's perfectly flat assessment of the situation as if this were mildly unusual rather than extraordinary.
jokes.explanation: A breezy line that lands as confirmation of Angel's excessive zeal. The understatement is functional.

jokes.text: My pen's running out. / Not a problem.
jokes.setup: Angel is laboriously processing a large number of detainees with diminishing resources.
jokes.punchline: Danny produces replacement pens from his person — an absurd quantity, suggesting he came prepared for exactly this. The visual of Danny producing pen after pen is the gag.
jokes.explanation: A quick visual/character beat establishing Danny's eagerness to please Angel and the absurdity of the situation. Functions as a bonding moment with comedic texture.

jokes.text: Lock me up. / I'm sorry? / I'm a slasher and I must be stopped. / You're a what? / A slasher of prices.
jokes.setup: A man walks in and says 'Lock me up. I'm a slasher and I must be stopped.' — entirely plausible as a confession of violence.
jokes.punchline: He runs the local supermarket. 'Slasher of prices.' The misdirection is deliberate and self-aware on Skinner's part.
jokes.explanation: Simon Skinner's introduction is very well written — the 'slasher of prices' line is an intentional double-meaning that doubles as a character statement (he makes jokes like this). Huge rewatch value given Skinner's eventual revealed nature. The structure is clean: scary setup, benign punchline, but the irony inverts completely on a second viewing.

jokes.text: Drop in and see me sometime. My discounts are criminal.
jokes.setup: Skinner is introducing himself to a police officer.
jokes.punchline: 'My discounts are criminal' — a retail pun that is also, for a police officer, an inadvertently (or deliberately) loaded word choice. Again, enormous rewatch irony.
jokes.explanation: A second Skinner wordplay-on-crime joke in quick succession — this one slightly weaker as the structure is identical but it reinforces his character voice. 'Criminal' doing double duty is good. The rewatch value is very high for this character specifically.

jokes.text: No. / Why? / He's not in yet. / Well, how's our guest? / Guest? / The inebriate in cell four. / I don't know. Nobody tells me nothing.
jokes.setup: Angel tries to get information from the front desk about basic station logistics.
jokes.punchline: 'Nobody tells me nothing' — the desk officer's cheerful admission that they're completely in the dark about their own station. It's also a double negative.
jokes.explanation: Light texture joke establishing the station's casual incompetence as a contrast to Angel's hyper-professionalism. Functional but unremarkable.

jokes.text: He's gone. / Oh, my God. Who's gone?
jokes.setup: Dramatic urgency as Danny announces 'He's gone' — implying a prisoner escape.
jokes.punchline: Nobody knows who 'he' refers to, deflating the drama instantly.
jokes.explanation: Quick deflation gag. Works as a beat but is structurally thin — the punchline is just 'nobody was paying attention.'

jokes.text: Why are you dressed like a police officer? / Because I am one.
jokes.setup: Angel apparently encounters Danny in a police uniform after last night's drunk driving incident — not expecting him to be an officer.
jokes.punchline: Danny is a police constable. Angel's assumption that the drunk he arrested couldn't be a cop is immediately and flatly corrected.
jokes.explanation: Clean setup/punchline with good character value — the reveal that the drunk is Angel's own colleague is efficiently handled. Danny's 'because I am one' is delivered with perfect guileless sincerity.

jokes.text: Speaking of which, that was a fair few outlaws you rounded up last night.
jokes.setup: Frank reveals he's a 'Wild West nut' and apologises for appearing in cowboy attire.
jokes.punchline: He immediately applies Wild West vocabulary ('outlaws you rounded up') to Angel's pub operation — framing Angel's excessive policing in cowboy terms.
jokes.explanation: A quick bit of character work for Butterman — the Wild West motif is introduced and immediately applied. Light but consistent.

jokes.text: Your predecessor assumed that rural policing was easy. Ended up having a nervous breakdown. And Sergeant Popwell was an exceptional officer, truly exceptional. And he had one thing you haven't got. / What's that, sir? / A great big bushy beard.
jokes.setup: Frank builds up the predecessor as 'exceptional' — Angel braces for a meaningful character comparison.
jokes.punchline: The differentiating factor is a beard. The elaborate setup for such a trivial punchline is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection/bathos: 'exceptional officer... had one thing you haven't got' builds to what should be wisdom or a character flaw, and delivers a beard. The long setup ('truly exceptional... one thing you haven't got') is well-calibrated to maximise the deflation. Good construction.

jokes.text: Now, how about a trip to the Andes? / Detective Sergeant Wainwright and Detective Constable Cartwright. / Don't get up. / I expect you're wondering why we call them the Andes. / They're both called Andrew? / They said you were good.
jokes.setup: Frank announces 'a trip to the Andes' — exotic and mysterious. Then introduces two detectives named Wainwright and Cartwright.
jokes.punchline: Angel immediately deduces the reason for the nickname ('They're both called Andrew?'). Frank's 'They said you were good' is both confirmation and compliment.
jokes.explanation: Elegant joke that shows Angel's detective brain firing on a linguistic puzzle, with Frank's appreciative 'They said you were good' as a perfect button. The setup ('trip to the Andes') is a confident misdirection, and Angel's deduction is satisfying to both Angel's character and the audience. Frank's response does double duty as both praise and punchline. Earns 8+ for multi-layer construction.

jokes.text: Also, because talking to them is an uphill struggle, isn't it, Dad? / Fuck off!
jokes.setup: Danny adds a second meaning to 'The Andes' nickname: it's also an uphill struggle.
jokes.punchline: The detective's immediate 'Fuck off' to Danny confirms both the accuracy of the description and the relationship dynamic.
jokes.explanation: The 'isn't it, Dad' and 'Fuck off' tandem lands well — it simultaneously extends the Andes joke, establishes Danny's lovable-idiot relationship with the station, and the bluntness of 'Fuck off' in polite company is funny. Danny saying 'isn't it, Dad' to a colleague reveals his social cluelessness.

jokes.text: She's our only policewoman. / She's not a policewoman. / Yeah, she is. I've seen her bra. / She's a police officer. Being a woman has nothing to do with it.
jokes.setup: Frank introduces Doris; Danny and Angel have a brief semantic dispute about 'policewoman' vs. 'police officer.'
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah, she is. I've seen her bra.' — Danny's empirical evidence for her being a woman is both technically irrelevant and wonderfully inappropriate. Angel corrects the terminology.
jokes.explanation: 'I've seen her bra' is a perfectly absurd piece of evidence that only Danny would offer. The structure mirrors the 'force/service' correction from earlier — Angel correcting language while missing the broader dynamic — but Danny's logic is so charmingly wrong-headed it stands alone. Good Danny character moment.

jokes.text: Oh, I don't know. Comes in handy every so often.
jokes.setup: Angel insists being a woman has nothing to do with being a police officer.
jokes.punchline: Doris cheerfully undermines the politically correct point with pragmatic self-interest.
jokes.explanation: A quick character introduction moment that positions Doris as pragmatically un-PC. Light but functional.

jokes.text: I could've given you the tour. I've been round the station a few times.
jokes.setup: Danny is trying to ingratiate himself with Angel throughout the tour.
jokes.punchline: His qualifications for giving the tour are that he's been there 'a few times' — not that he works there, not that he knows it well, just that he's been round it.
jokes.explanation: Light Danny character moment. The slight implication that his credentials are thin is consistent with his character but doesn't punch hard.

jokes.text: It's a pity you didn't do the same to those bloody hoodies. Hanging around. Loitering. Sitting.
jokes.setup: Tom Weaver, the officious Neighbourhood Watch head, praises Angel's arrests but laments the hoodies are still at large.
jokes.punchline: 'Hanging around. Loitering. Sitting.' — the escalating list of criminal activities culminates in 'sitting' as the most dangerous offence, perfectly skewering Daily Mail-style paranoia.
jokes.explanation: Very well-calibrated satirical joke. The list structure — 'hanging around / loitering / sitting' — appears to build toward something serious before revealing that 'sitting' is the apex crime. It precisely captures the paranoid logic of neighbourhood watch overreach. Character integration is high because only Weaver's worldview produces this list.

jokes.text: If we don't come down hard on these clowns, we are gonna be up to our balls in jugglers.
jokes.setup: Weaver is raging about street performers — specifically The Living Statue.
jokes.punchline: The catastrophising logic: tolerate one statue, and jugglers will follow. 'Up to our balls in jugglers' is both vivid and absurd.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. 'Up to our balls in jugglers' is a perfect absurdist image delivered with complete conviction. The slippery-slope logic (clown → juggler infestation) is both a great character joke for Weaver and a sharp satire on moral panic. High quotability — this is a line audiences quote. The vividness of 'balls in jugglers' is unexpected and sharp.

jokes.text: We like to let them think they run the place.
jokes.setup: Tom Weaver delivers his paranoid diatribe and Frank promises action.
jokes.punchline: Frank explains quietly to Angel that they humour Weaver — 'we like to let them think they run the place' — a line that is funny now and deeply sinister on rewatch.
jokes.explanation: A line with significant dramatic irony given later revelations about who actually runs Sandford. On first watch it's a mild joke about managing busybodies; on rewatch it's a revealing window into the actual power structure. Good economy and high rewatch value.

jokes.text: Yes, sir. Why is everybody eating chocolate cake?
jokes.setup: Frank asks if there's anything Angel is unclear about — presumably expecting operational questions.
jokes.punchline: Angel's question is about the cake. After everything he's been briefed on, this is what he notices.
jokes.explanation: A good observational beat — after all the institutional madness, Angel's precise observational instinct latches onto the irrelevant detail of mass cake consumption. Sets up the punishment explanation well.

jokes.text: The Black Forest gateau is on Danny. As punishment for his little indiscretion. / His... Sir, I don't think driving under the influence can be called a 'little indiscretion.' / No, the gateau is for misplacing his helmet the other week. Last night's incident will require something rather more serious.
jokes.setup: Angel assumes the punishment cake is for the DUI — which would be absurdly lenient.
jokes.punchline: Frank clarifies: the cake is for a different, minor infraction. The DUI will get something 'more serious' — implying an even more elaborate food punishment. The triviality of the punishment system is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Nicely structured: Angel's objection ('can't be called a little indiscretion') is correct but misapplied — the cake is for something even more trivial. The pivot is clean and the revelation that the station runs on confectionary punishment is a good worldbuilding joke.

jokes.text: Good. / Do you like ice-cream? / I'm sorry, sir, I don't follow. / Let's just say that we won't be short of Chunky Monkey for the next month.
jokes.setup: Angel approves of a 'more serious' punishment.
jokes.punchline: The 'more serious' punishment is apparently a large quantity of Ben & Jerry's ice cream. The confectionary justice system escalates from cake to ice cream.
jokes.explanation: 'Chunky Monkey' is a good specific choice — it's a recognisable brand name that sounds both indulgent and slightly ridiculous. The escalation from gateau to Chunky Monkey maintains the joke's internal logic while extending it. Danny's 'Dad' is a good button.

jokes.text: So, what made you choose Sandford then, Sergeant Angel? / It wasn't actually my choice. / Oh, right, right, wasn't your choice to come down here and tell me how to do my job. / Our jobs.
jokes.setup: Danny asks a seemingly innocent question about Angel's choice to come to Sandford.
jokes.punchline: Angel corrects 'my job' to 'our jobs' — a small territorial detail that reveals Danny's underlying resentment about Angel's arrival, while Angel's correction is both legalistic and inadvertently provocative.
jokes.explanation: Light friction between the two leads, establishes dynamics. The 'our jobs' correction is functional character work without being a killer joke.

jokes.text: Look, I can assure you it wasn't my intention to upset the apple cart. / Yeah, 'cause we all sell apples round here, don't we? / Your dad sells apples, Andy. / And raspberries.
jokes.setup: Angel uses the idiom 'upset the apple cart.'
jokes.punchline: PC Andy takes it literally (or pretends to), pointing out that apple selling is literally common in the village; the other Andy adds 'and raspberries' with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: 'And raspberries' is the button that makes the joke — the second Andy confirming the fruit inventory with total seriousness extends the literalism perfectly. A good idiomatic/literal play.

jokes.text: I bet you can't wait to jump into Sergeant Popwell's grave.
jokes.setup: Angel is being subtly resented by the team for taking over.
jokes.punchline: Fisher's accusation uses a dark idiom that's both literally wrong (Popwell had a breakdown, didn't die) and metaphorically hostile — the aggression is wrapped in a cliché.
jokes.explanation: More of a character beat than a great joke — Fisher's hostility is noted, the slight inapplicability of the 'grave' idiom (Popwell isn't dead) is a minor wrinkle. Functional.

jokes.text: You got a mustache. / I know. / Why have you got your stab vest on? / It's a requirement. / In the city maybe. Nobody's gonna stab you in here, Sergeant. / Not a member of the public anyhow.
jokes.setup: Angel's London-cop habits (stab vest) are mocked as over-cautious in sleepy Sandford.
jokes.punchline: Fisher's 'not a member of the public anyhow' implies that Angel might be stabbed by a colleague — a dark joke that's also a threat.
jokes.explanation: Fisher's line is genuinely menacing under the comedic surface, which gives it a dark subversive edge consistent with the film's genre. The aside 'not a member of the public anyhow' is delivered as a throwaway but lands as a threat. High rewatch value given later events.

jokes.text: Have you been stabbed, Sergeant Fisher? / No. / Well, I have. And I can assure you it is not in the least bit amusing.
jokes.setup: Fisher and colleagues mock Angel's stab vest as unnecessary.
jokes.punchline: Angel's confirmation that he has been stabbed, delivered with exquisite formality: 'I can assure you it is not in the least bit amusing.' The understatement carries the comedy.
jokes.explanation: 'Not in the least bit amusing' is a beautiful piece of Angelic understatement — the gap between the gravity of being stabbed and the prim formality of the complaint is very funny. Character integration is high because this is exactly how Angel expresses everything. Shaun of the Dead DNA here.

jokes.text: Have you seen a lot of action? / I've experienced my fair share, yes. / Did you cook any fools? / Excuse me? / Did you shoot anybody? / He shot a crack head with a Kalashnikov. / Where did you get that? / The offender had the Kalashnikov.
jokes.setup: Officers probe Angel about his combat history using slang ('cook any fools') that Angel doesn't understand.
jokes.punchline: The clarification that the offender, not Angel, had the Kalashnikov is a funny deflation — Angel didn't bring an AK-47 to work, he was up against one.
jokes.explanation: Light texture exchange; the deflation of 'the offender had the Kalashnikov' is clean but the setup is fairly standard 'city cop vs country yokels' territory.

jokes.text: Where'd he get that? / You do know there are more guns in the country than there are in the city? Everybody and their mums is packing round here. / Like who? / Farmers. / Who else? / Farmers's mums.
jokes.setup: Officers claim rural areas are more heavily armed than the city, which seems implausible.
jokes.punchline: The only examples are farmers and 'farmers's mums' — both armed with the same demographic precision, which is simultaneously specific and useless.
jokes.explanation: 'Farmers's mums' is a great punchline — the specificity of the sub-category, delivered with equal confidence, is absurdist and perfectly economical. The escalation from 'farmers' to 'farmers's mums' follows a perfect logic. This line is quotable and has the right snap.

jokes.text: What's it like being stabbed? / It was the single most painful experience of my life. / What was the second most painful?
jokes.setup: Danny asks about being stabbed — apparently fascinated by Angel's combat history.
jokes.punchline: Angel gives a grave, sincere answer about it being the most painful experience. Danny follows with 'What was the second most painful?' — an entirely reasonable follow-up question that is somehow funnier than a punchline.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Danny's question is both logical and inappropriate — he treats Angel's trauma as a conversation-starting ranking exercise. The beat [20:42–20:50] where Angel presumably stares at him before answering sells it. Danny's clueless enthusiasm is perfectly pitched.

jokes.text: [Angel's silent reaction / pause] after 'What was the second most painful?'
jokes.setup: Danny asks for the ranking of Angel's most painful experiences.
jokes.punchline: Angel's pause — suggesting the second most painful is something personal and embarrassing (presumably the breakup or the transfer) — is funnier than any answer.
jokes.explanation: The pause after Danny's question is the punchline — silence is the best answer. Edgar Wright knows when not to give the audience the explicit joke and lets them fill it in. The audience's imagination (the breakup? the transfer?) is funnier than any specific answer. Perfect economy in the purest sense.

jokes.text: You ever fired two guns whilst jumping through the air? / No. / You ever fired one gun whilst jumping through the air? / No. / Ever been in a high speed pursuit? / Yes, I have. / You ever fired a gun whilst in a high speed pursuit? / No.
jokes.setup: Danny is essentially quizzing Angel on action-movie tropes, expecting a real-life hero.
jokes.punchline: The sequence of increasingly specific action-film scenarios — two guns in mid-air, one gun in mid-air, gun in pursuit — all deflated with flat 'No's. The lone 'yes' (high speed pursuit) makes the follow-up 'No' (gun during pursuit) funnier.
jokes.explanation: This sequence is the film establishing its action-movie obsession through Danny's hero worship. The structure is excellent: escalating absurdity, the one real 'yes' creating false hope, then crushed. 'Two guns whilst jumping through the air' is a deliberately specific action-movie citation. High rewatch value as it foreshadows the film's climax.

jokes.text: You ever fired two guns whilst jumping through the air? / No. / You ever fired one gun whilst jumping through the air? / No. / Ever been in a high speed pursuit? / Yes, I have. / You ever fired a gun whilst in a high speed pursuit? / No.
jokes.setup: Danny interrogates Angel about action-movie policing tropes.
jokes.punchline: The escalating specificity of action-movie scenarios — culminating in the technically-possible-but-still-absurd combination — punctuated by Angel's flat 'No' to each one.
jokes.explanation: Excellent setup for Danny's character — his world of reference is entirely action movies. The rewatch bonus is significant because these questions become a checklist the film itself eventually fulfills. Angel's patient 'No' to each escalating fantasy is the perfect straight-man response. The one 'Yes' (high-speed pursuit) quickly deflated by another 'No' is structurally smart.

jokes.text: Annette, that Sergeant Angel's coming into your shop. Get a look at his arse.
jokes.setup: Angel is apparently walking through the village being watched by residents.
jokes.punchline: A villager is radio-broadcasting Angel's approach and instructing another to appraise his backside — the village surveillance network is used for this.
jokes.explanation: Good texture joke — the village surveillance introduced earlier (Tom Weaver's cameras) is repurposed for community objectification of Angel. It's a quick laugh that also develops the village's hive-mind observation quality.

jokes.text: What about Lethal Weapon? / No. / You've seen Die Hard, though? / No. / Bad Boys II? / No. / You ain't seen Bad Boys II?
jokes.setup: Following the action-film quiz, Danny now probes Angel's film literacy.
jokes.punchline: The escalating disbelief as Angel hasn't seen any of them, culminating in Danny's scandalized 'You ain't seen Bad Boys II?' — his greatest shock is reserved for Bad Boys II specifically, which is both very specific and slightly deflating.
jokes.explanation: The specific choice of Bad Boys II as the apex of Danny's cinematic canon is brilliantly calibrated — it's not Die Hard (too obvious) or Lethal Weapon (too prestige), but Bad Boys II, which is precisely the kind of film a Danny Butterman would hold sacred. His 'you ain't seen Bad Boys II?' has the energy of genuine cultural horror. High quotability. Establishes the film's central relationship dynamic efficiently.

jokes.text: Nicholas, hello. Reverend Shooter. / I want to ask you, would you read a homily at Sunday Service? / That might be a little hypocritical of me, Reverend. / Oh, you're an atheist? / No, I'm… I'm… I'm open to the concept of religion, I'm just not entirely convinced by it. / You're an agnostic? / I think I have a cream for that.
jokes.setup: Angel carefully defines himself as agnostic, distinguishing from atheism with awkward hedging.
jokes.punchline: Hatcher mishears 'agnostic' as a skin condition and offers a cream — the perfect deadpan medical misunderstanding.
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the reel. The setup is elaborate and pays off beautifully: Angel's careful philosophical hedging is interrupted by Hatcher's completely literal medical interpretation. 'I think I have a cream for that' is a brilliantly timed non-sequitur that's perfectly in character for a doctor, and the agnostic/skin-condition confusion is a great wordplay misdirect. Earns 8+ for structure, economy, and quotability.

jokes.text: Oh, you're an atheist? / No, I'm... I'm open to the concept of religion, I'm just not entirely convinced by it. / You're an agnostic? / I think I have a cream for that.
jokes.setup: Angel carefully explains his nuanced theological position: open to religion, not convinced.
jokes.punchline: Dr. Hatcher mishears 'agnostic' as a medical condition — 'I think I have a cream for that.'
jokes.explanation: 'I think I have a cream for that' is a quotable, well-timed gag — the doctor mishearing a theological term as a skin complaint is a good character joke (doctor sees everything as medical) and a good phonetic joke. The setup through the Reverend asking and Angel's careful hedging makes the punchline land harder. High quotability.

jokes.text: I am sure that all of you will have noticed the return of a blight to our streets... I refer, of course, to the extremely irritating Living Statue.
jokes.setup: Weaver announces a 'blight' — building urgency and dread before the reveal.
jokes.punchline: 'The extremely irritating Living Statue' — the punchline deflates the buildup with a street performer rather than any actual threat.
jokes.explanation: A callback to the earlier mention of the Living Statue in the command centre. The bathos of presenting a mime as a civic emergency is consistent with Weaver's character. Decent but doesn't add much beyond the first mention.

jokes.text: Police work is as much about preventing crime as it is about fighting crime. Most importantly, it is about procedural correctness in the execution of unquestionable moral authority. / Any questions? / Yes. / Is it true that there is a place in a man's head that if you shoot it, it will blow up?
jokes.setup: Angel delivers a sincere, earnest speech about police work to schoolchildren, inviting questions.
jokes.punchline: A child asks whether a headshot causes the head to explode — a question that could only come from video games or action movies. Angel's reaction beat is the secondary payoff.
jokes.explanation: The gravity of Angel's speech and the Q&A format create an expectation of an earnest or thoughtful question. The specific wording — 'a place in a man's head that if you shoot it, it will blow up' — is delivered with the child's total seriousness, which is what makes it funny. Good misdirection structure.

jokes.text: Hi, hi, Tim Messenger. Can I get a quick shot for the Sandford Citizen? / Okay. / How about you put the teacher in handcuffs? / I don't think that gives off the right signals. / Too cheesy-pie. Okay. Gotcha. / Give the little blonde kid your hat. / I'd rather not. / Wave your hitting stick about. / No. / Righty-ho-ho.
jokes.setup: Local journalist Tim Messenger wants a photo op and pitches increasingly inappropriate suggestions.
jokes.punchline: Each escalating request ('handcuffs on teacher / give kid your hat / wave your hitting stick') is refused with equal flatness; Messenger's 'Righty-ho-ho' accepts defeat with inexplicable cheerfulness.
jokes.explanation: Tim Messenger is a great recurring character type — the provincial journalist with no editorial judgment. 'Wave your hitting stick about' is the best of the suggestions (the euphemism for a truncheon is fantastic). 'Righty-ho-ho' as a sign-off is good character work. Escalation sequence works.

jokes.text: Hi, hi, Tim Messenger. Can I get a quick shot for the Sandford Citizen? / How about you put the teacher in handcuffs? / I don't think that gives off the right signals. / Too cheesy-pie. Okay. Gotcha. / Give the little blonde kid your hat. / I'd rather not. / Wave your hitting stick about. / No.
jokes.setup: Local journalist Tim Messenger tries to stage a photo with Angel.
jokes.punchline: Each suggestion is worse than the last (handcuffs, hat, 'hitting stick') — escalating tabloid ridiculousness met with Angel's flat refusals.
jokes.explanation: 'Wave your hitting stick about' is the best of the three suggestions — 'hitting stick' as a baton euphemism is an excellent Messenger-character detail. Angel's patient 'No' mirrors the earlier triple refusal from his demotion. Good character-comedy escalation.

jokes.text: Morning, Angle. / Good morning, Angle. / Morning, Angle. / Morning, Angle. / Sergeant Angel. / Morning. The swan's escaped.
jokes.setup: Multiple villagers greet Angel, all mispronouncing his name as 'Angle.'
jokes.punchline: He corrects the last one — and is immediately answered with the trivial emergency of an escaped swan.
jokes.explanation: The 'Angle' mispronunciation running gag is good world texture but individually the beats are modest. The transition to swan emergency is good deflation.

jokes.text: Mr. Staker. Yeah, Mr. Peter Ian Staker. / P.I. Staker. Right. Piss taker. Come on!
jokes.setup: A man introduces himself as Peter Ian Staker — his full name sounds unremarkable.
jokes.punchline: P.I. Staker. Angel (and audience) clock the initials: Piss Taker. Angel assumes it's a prank. 'Come on!'
jokes.explanation: Classic initials/name joke — P.I. Staker / Pisstaker. The payoff is that the man is completely genuine. The delivery of Angel's incredulous 'Come on!' followed by the man providing a detailed swan description is a good structural joke. Rewatch value because the deadpan continuation sells it.

jokes.text: Yes, Mr. Staker. We'll do everything we can. Can you describe it to me? / It's about two foot tall. Long slender neck. Kind of orange and black bill. Anything else? / Well, it's a swan.
jokes.setup: Angel professionally asks for a description of the escaped animal — treating it with full police procedure.
jokes.punchline: 'Well, it's a swan.' — after a detailed physical description, the man's final observation is that it looks like a swan. It's the least useful additional information possible, delivered as if it were helpful.
jokes.explanation: The punchline is the film's last joke in this reel and it's one of the best executed. Angel applies full professional police procedure to a lost-swan report, complete with physical description prompt; the man's answer — 'well, it's a swan' — is both tautological and sincere. The build-and-deflate is clean, the economy is excellent. A very satisfying reel-closer.

jokes.text: - No luck catching them swans then? - It's just the one swan, actually.
jokes.setup: Danny asks casually about 'them swans' — implying a plural, chaotic pursuit
jokes.punchline: Angel's pedantic correction ('It's just the one swan, actually') immediately establishes his obsessive precision while deflating the heroic image
jokes.explanation: A deceptively rich joke: Danny's casual plural implies mayhem, Angel's precise singular correction is both funny on its own and deeply character-revealing. The economy is exceptional — eight words do enormous work establishing Angel's pedantry, the absurdity of the police situation, and the comedic dynamic between the two leads. High rewatch value because on second viewing you realize this is a character thesis statement disguised as a throwaway line.

jokes.text: - Want anything from the shop? - You've just been to the shop. / I was thinking of a different shop.
jokes.setup: Danny immediately asks about going to another shop right after returning from one
jokes.punchline: 'I was thinking of a different shop' — the non-justification is itself the joke, revealing Danny's idle, food-obsessed nature
jokes.explanation: Clean, economic character comedy. 'A different shop' works because it offers no actual justification — Danny's logic is entirely self-sufficient and self-defeating. Efficiently codes him as a simple, comfort-seeking man-child against Angel's driven professionalism.

jokes.text: Angel spots Mr. Treacher and speculates: 'Why has he got that big coat on? He can't be cold. Why the extra layer? Maybe he's trying to hide something.'
jokes.setup: Angel tries to teach Danny to look for suspicious behavior in the mundane village
jokes.punchline: The 'suspicious' behavior is an old man wearing a coat — Angel's hyperactive detective instinct is hilariously over-applied to nothing
jokes.explanation: Good running setup for the 'suspicious villager' bit. Angel's urban-cop paranoia clashing with rural innocuousness is core to the film's comedic premise. The joke itself is mild but serves as the first beat in an escalating sequence.

jokes.text: Angel: 'Ask yourself, why has he got his hat pulled down like that?' Danny: 'He's fuck ugly.' Angel: 'Or he doesn't want you to see his face.' Danny: 'Because he's fuck ugly.'
jokes.setup: Angel tries to teach Danny to look for sinister motivations in suspicious appearances
jokes.punchline: Danny's blunt 'he's fuck ugly' twice obliterates Angel's conspiratorial reasoning with crude Occam's razor logic
jokes.explanation: The doubling is what makes it work: Danny says 'he's fuck ugly,' Angel tries to reframe it as suspicious concealment, and Danny just re-states the same answer. The structure is a perfect comedic two-beat with the punchline winning by repetition rather than escalation. Character-integrated — only Danny would flatten sophisticated detective logic this bluntly. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Exchange about Lurch's mum and sister being 'the same person'
jokes.setup: Angel asks if Lurch's mum and sister are as big as he is — a casual question about family
jokes.punchline: Danny reveals with total nonchalance that the mum and sister are the same person — implying incest
jokes.explanation: Classic dark-reveal punchline delivered with maximum economy and nonchalance. Danny doesn't react to what he's just implied — the horror is entirely in the audience's inference. The pivot to 'What shop were you thinking of?' is a perfect button, resetting the previous thread as if nothing happened.

jokes.text: 'What shop were you thinking of?' — Angel's immediate pivot back to the shop conversation after the incest revelation
jokes.setup: Danny has just casually implied his acquaintance's mum and sister are the same person
jokes.punchline: Angel ignores the horrifying implication entirely and returns to the trivial shop question — his priorities are inscrutable
jokes.explanation: Perfect button joke. The script circles back to the shop thread only after the incest reveal, making the juxtaposition the joke. Angel's complete non-reaction to the dark content and pivot to the mundane is a masterclass in comedic timing via script structure. High rewatch bonus — you catch the full architecture the second time.

jokes.text: PA announcement: 'Sergeant Angel. Or is it Angle?'
jokes.setup: Supermarket PA calls for 'Sergeant Angel' to come to the manager's office
jokes.punchline: The announcer immediately second-guesses herself — 'Or is it Angle?' — mispronouncing his name in a passive-aggressive or genuinely confused way
jokes.explanation: Mild but functional gag. The deliberate second-guess introduces the village's passive resistance to Angel before he even meets them properly. Not particularly original but efficient.

jokes.text: Mr. Skinner to Michael (Lurch): 'Child vomit. Aisle six. Mop it up.' Michael: 'Yarp.'
jokes.setup: Michael Armstrong (Lurch) was just established as having 'a child's mind'; he's now being directed like a machine
jokes.punchline: 'Yarp' — his only word, used as full affirmative response to the most degrading possible assignment, delivered without affect
jokes.explanation: 'Yarp' is a running gag with high payoff every deployment. Used here to comic effect as the total monosyllabic acceptance of an awful job. The specificity of 'child vomit' elevates it. High quotability — 'Yarp' has become genuinely iconic from this film.

jokes.text: Skinner re defectors to the Megamart: 'May their heads be struck from their shoulders for such disloyalty.'
jokes.setup: Skinner is performing gracious hospitality, talking about loyalty to the local store in mild retail terms
jokes.punchline: He suddenly escalates to medieval decapitation as the appropriate punishment for shopping elsewhere — delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: Excellent foreshadowing-as-joke. The disproportionate medieval violence applied to petty retail disloyalty is funny on the surface, but on rewatch this is a chilling hint at Skinner's true nature. The deadpan delivery is crucial — if he winked at the audience it would die. Character-integrated because only someone with Skinner's suppressed fanaticism would phrase it this way. Rewatch bonus is high.

jokes.text: Angel in the supermarket produces a subtle redirect — 'Well, maybe I'm not the one you should be keeping an eye on' — intending to flag a suspicious person; Skinner thinks he means George Merchant
jokes.setup: Angel suggests Skinner should watch someone else — implying a known local criminal type
jokes.punchline: Skinner immediately takes it as an invitation to gossip about the 'Fridge Magnate' George Merchant — entirely missing Angel's intended implication
jokes.explanation: Functional misdirection gag. The gap between what Angel means and what Skinner hears is a mild double-meaning joke. It's more plot-mechanical than comic but earns a smile.

jokes.text: Action movie poster: 'Meet the cop that can't be stopped' — shown while Angel is jogging in the village
jokes.setup: Angel is on a mundane morning jog through a sleepy English village
jokes.punchline: The action-movie tagline on a poster he passes hyper-ironically describes a man currently doing nothing dramatic whatsoever
jokes.explanation: Classic Edgar Wright visual gag — the film's own genre commenting on itself. The irony of an action-movie supercop jogging past his own poster in a dull village is on-brand. Rewatch bonus because it recurs as a motif.

jokes.text: 'Tosser!' — shouted as Angel pursues a shoplifter through the village; radio crackles with 'Sergeant Angel's having a spot of bother'
jokes.setup: Angel is in the middle of an action-movie-style chase through a quiet English village
jokes.punchline: The radio description 'a spot of bother' — British understatement at maximum — reduces a full foot-pursuit to a cup-of-tea problem
jokes.explanation: 'A spot of bother' as the radio description of a hot pursuit is a crisp understatement joke. Works well contextually as the chase scene is played straight but narrated as trivial.

jokes.text: 'What's the matter, Danny? You never taken a shortcut before?' — Angel and Danny vault through private gardens in a hyperactive chase sequence
jokes.setup: The chase through gardens is a loving recreation of the Point Break / action movie garden-hopping chase Angel will later reference explicitly
jokes.punchline: Angel's breathless quip while actively recreating the scene he's about to describe — the film is self-consciously constructing the callback it will pay off in seconds
jokes.explanation: Edgar Wright structuring comedy in advance of its own payoff — the film stages the Point Break reference before Angel names it. The chase is both a genuine parody of action sequences and a stealth setup. Rewatch bonus is significant here.

jokes.text: 'And it didn't occur to you to mention this before?' / 'Couldn't see his face, could I? I'm not made of eyes.'
jokes.setup: Angel is exasperated that Danny didn't flag the connection during the chase
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not made of eyes' — an utterly bizarre non-sequitur logic that somehow makes internal sense only to Danny
jokes.explanation: 'I'm not made of eyes' is one of the best lines in this reel. It's absurdist self-defense that is somehow both completely wrong (eyes are on faces, not distributed across your body) and weirdly logical (he couldn't see the face from behind). The phrase has a dreamlike wrongness to it that makes it instantly quotable. It's deeply character-specific — only Danny would defend himself with an accidental body-horror image. Comparable in quotability and surprise to the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: Shame Mr. Skinner doesn't want to press charges. / ... / Stealing biscuits is wrong? / Correct. / Thanks.
jokes.setup: Nicholas expects a serious consequence for the shoplifter; the Inspector suggests Peter be given a second chance to 'learn a valuable lesson'
jokes.punchline: Nicholas sarcastically summarizes: 'Stealing biscuits is wrong?' — and the Inspector confirms it, deadpan. Peter then thanks them, oblivious to the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Good layered joke — Nicholas's sarcasm, the Inspector's earnest confirmation, and Peter's clueless 'thanks' are three distinct comic beats landing in quick succession. The small-town law enforcement parody is well-executed.

jokes.text: 'Well, that's the way the cookie crumbles.' / 'Like the biscuits, isn't it?'
jokes.setup: Angel protests that the shoplifter (who stole biscuits) is not being charged — Inspector Butterman dismisses it with a cliché
jokes.punchline: Danny cheerfully literalizes the idiom by pointing out it refers to cookies/biscuits — exactly what was stolen — turning a dismissive cliché into an accidental perfect metaphor
jokes.explanation: Elegant wordplay gag: the cliché accidentally applies to the literal situation. Danny's delight in the coincidence ('Like the biscuits, isn't it?') is better than any straight joke could be. Well-structured two-beat.

jokes.text: Angel doing chin-ups in the jail cell while Danny keeps count — Angel asks Danny about Point Break
jokes.setup: Angel is apparently exercising on the jail bars while having a casual conversation about action movies
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of obsessive physical discipline with a pop-culture movie chat about Point Break creates an absurd domesticity
jokes.explanation: Functional scene-setting comedy. The visual of Angel doing chin-ups while Danny earnestly pitches Point Break is funny primarily as atmosphere and character contrast. The numbers punctuating Danny's monologue are good rhythmic comedy, though.

jokes.text: Danny's breathless Point Break pitch: 'Patrick Swayze's just robbed this bank and Keanu Reeves is chasing him through people's gardens, and he goes to shoot Swayze but he can't, 'cause he loves him so much, and he's firing his gun up in the air, he's like...'
jokes.setup: Danny is trying to sell Angel on Point Break immediately after they just ran through people's gardens in a chase
jokes.punchline: The film has just recreated the exact scene Danny is describing — the audience has already seen the garden-chase, so Danny's wide-eyed summary is a meta-callback to what just happened on screen
jokes.explanation: This is Edgar Wright's structural comedy at its best: the film stages a parody of Point Break's garden chase, then immediately has Danny describe the scene in innocent admiration — without realizing he's just lived it. The payoff to the garden-chase setup is enormous, and the structure (do the thing, then describe the thing) is impeccable. This is the kind of joke that gets better every rewatch because you see the architecture. The 'he loves him so much' detail about why Keanu can't shoot is an additional character-comedy gem. Genuinely exceptional writing.

jokes.text: 'Have you ever fired your gun up in the air and gone...' / 'No, I have not ever fired my gun up in the air and gone...'
jokes.setup: Danny impersonates Keanu Reeves firing into the air — implying a wordless anguished 'AAARGH' — and asks if Angel has done this
jokes.punchline: Angel repeats the exact same phrase back ('No, I have not ever fired my gun up in the air and gone...') leaving the imagined sound effect conspicuously unvoiced — the absence of the sound IS the joke
jokes.explanation: One of the film's signature jokes and a canonical Hot Fuzz moment. The setup and punchline leave the actual gun-noise unprintable in a subtitle transcript, but its absence in both Danny's question and Angel's precise parroting back creates a shared imaginary scream. The parallel structure — Angel mirroring Danny's exact words — is both a character moment (Angel's pedantry) and the perfect comedic vehicle. It has become the film's most quoted exchange. Well above 8.0 anchor quality.

jokes.text: 'I wanna do what you do.' / 'You do, do what I do.'
jokes.setup: Danny expresses admiration for Angel's police work
jokes.punchline: Angel's literal, slightly impatient parsing of 'do what you do' — 'You do, do what I do' — creates a momentary tongue-twister of deadpan logic
jokes.explanation: Quick, clean wordplay. Angel's pedantic reparse of Danny's idiom into a slightly absurd literal statement is funny but brief. Good economy.

jokes.text: 'Police work is not about proper action or shit.'
jokes.setup: Danny lists what he wants: 'Gun fights. Car chases. Proper action and shit.'
jokes.punchline: Angel's prim, precise dismissal uses the word 'shit' in a formal sentence — the incongruity of register is the joke
jokes.explanation: Angel quoting back Danny's phrase 'and shit' in his crisp official-speak voice is a good register-clash joke. Brief but effective.

jokes.text: 'Fire up the roof.' — Angel apparently engages some dramatic police vehicle feature mid-lecture about how police work isn't dramatic
jokes.setup: Angel has just lectured Danny that police work isn't about 'proper action or shit'
jokes.punchline: He immediately hits 'fire up the roof' — activating sirens/lights on the car — directly contradicting his own speech with an action-movie flourish
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic reversal. Angel delivers a straight-faced lecture about how police work isn't dramatic, then immediately does the dramatically cool thing. The structure is immaculate: statement → immediate contradiction in action. Danny's 'That was brilliant' response is a great button — his admiration is exactly the reaction Angel is denying wanting. Very well constructed.

jokes.text: Mr. Blower: 'I'm playing the eponymous hero, you see. Romeo not Juliet.'
jokes.setup: Blower has been pulled over for speeding and explains he's late for a Romeo and Juliet rehearsal — Angel writes everything down
jokes.punchline: 'Romeo not Juliet' — his anxious clarification that he's not playing the girl role is an absurd defensive non-sequitur delivered as though it's vital legal information
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical character joke. Blower, panicking under Angel's relentless note-taking, defensively clarifies his gender. The word 'eponymous' doing heavy lifting: a pompous man using an obscure word while confessing to something trivially embarrassing. The clarification is funnier than any insult could be.

jokes.text: Angel: 'What are you writing?' / Angel: 'Everything you're saying. I might need to refer to it later.' — leading Blower to panic and demand he stop
jokes.setup: Blower is explaining his speeding excuse; Angel silently writes in his notebook
jokes.punchline: Angel confirms he's recording everything verbatim — the mundane professionalism becomes a form of quiet menace that rattles Blower completely
jokes.explanation: Good cringe-comedy. Angel's notebook transforms bureaucratic procedure into a form of psychological pressure. The power dynamic is inverted — the pompous solicitor becomes increasingly flustered by a cop just doing paperwork. Character-specific: Angel's professionalism as his weapon.

jokes.text: Angel asks to see Danny's notebook — Danny reveals it's full of doodles
jokes.setup: Angel has just demonstrated how the notebook saves his skin; he lectures Danny on using his
jokes.punchline: Danny's notebook, supposedly a police tool, is revealed to be entirely filled with drawings — the contrast with Angel's meticulous record-keeping is total
jokes.explanation: Solid visual gag. The reveal of Danny's doodle-filled notebook against Angel's crisp professional one is a perfect one-image character contrast. Danny's 'You should see the one on the other side' as a proud response is a good button.

jokes.text: 'That's just extraordinary.' — Angel's reaction to the doodle notebook / Danny: 'You should see the one on the other side.'
jokes.setup: Angel reviews Danny's notebook expecting police notes
jokes.punchline: Danny's proud follow-up 'You should see the one on the other side' implies the doodles continue — and are apparently even better — his complete lack of shame being the joke
jokes.explanation: Good button on the notebook gag. Danny's pride in his doodles is consistent with his character and the 'other side' teaser functions as a callback setup for rewatch.

jokes.text: Angel declines going to the pub: 'I have to water my Peace Lily.'
jokes.setup: Danny suggests they do something that evening — pub perhaps
jokes.punchline: Angel's excuse is watering a Peace Lily — a pitifully domestic, solitary reason that underlines his social isolation in Sandford
jokes.explanation: The Peace Lily is a perfect specific detail. It's not just 'I have to stay in' — it's a named plant that conjures the image of this serious cop alone in a bare flat talking to a flower. Good character economy.

jokes.text: Romeo shoots himself with a prop gun: 'Bang!'
jokes.setup: The am-dram Romeo and Juliet is being staged; Blower is playing Romeo and has just been established as a pompous solicitor
jokes.punchline: His death scene involves a cheerful 'Bang!' — the amateur theatrics of the gesture undercuts Shakespeare's tragedy completely
jokes.explanation: Funny visual: a pompous man's gun-prop death in Shakespeare. Gains major rewatch value because Blower will die shortly in a car crash, giving 'Bang!' a very dark retroactive resonance.

jokes.text: Reporter Simon Skinner pitches headlines: 'Cop Enjoys Watching Young Lovers' / 'Local Bobby Gives Thumbs Up To Teen Suicide'
jokes.setup: Reporter approaches Angel after the am-dram for a quote about enjoying Romeo and Juliet
jokes.punchline: His headline suggestions are grotesquely inappropriate reframings of 'policeman enjoyed the play' — tabloid logic taken to absurdist extreme
jokes.explanation: Two perfectly escalating dark headlines. The structure — suggesting interpretations that are technically accurate but sensationally awful — is a sharp satire of tabloid journalism. 'Teen Suicide' as a headline for Angel enjoying a Shakespeare play is the funnier of the two, with good escalation between them. Highly quotable. Angel's straight 'That's just grossly inappropriate' is the ideal non-reaction.

jokes.text: 'Greg over there was an extra in Straw Dogs and Sheree portrayed a cadaver in Prime Suspect.'
jokes.setup: Butterman is reassuring Angel that the 'professional actor' understudies are impressive credentials
jokes.punchline: The credentials are vanishingly minor — an extra and a corpse — delivered with total pride
jokes.explanation: Classic English-village status comedy: being an extra in Straw Dogs is somehow a credential. The escalation from 'extra' to 'portrayed a cadaver' (which requires nothing of the actor) is perfectly chosen, with 'portrayed' being the best word choice — she did not 'play' or 'appear as' but 'portrayed' a dead body.

jokes.text: 'I'm sure if we bashed your head in, all sorts of secrets would come tumbling out.'
jokes.setup: Blower is introducing Eve Draper as someone who knows local council secrets
jokes.punchline: His playful/aggressive metaphor for getting information — literally bashing her head in — is delivered as a flirtatious social nicety
jokes.explanation: Deceptively dark. On first view: a slightly odd compliment. On rewatch: a chilling foreshadowing of exactly how Blower/the NWA operates. The rewatch bonus is significant — this is Wright using comedy as a horror plant. The register of casual social charm around graphic violence is the film's signature trick.

jokes.text: 'Romeo, Romeo, a pint of bitter for Romeo?' — pub landlord calling Blower's drink order
jokes.setup: Blower has just been playing Romeo on stage; the pub landlord uses his character name
jokes.punchline: The Shakespeare invocation of 'Romeo, Romeo' applied to a pint-order is a perfect deflation of Blower's theatrical self-importance
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. The landlord using the balcony-scene invocation to call time on a pint is a sharp, quick wordplay gag that earns a solid laugh through sheer elegance.

jokes.text: Angel: 'She clearly has a thing for older men.' / Danny: 'What, with Martin Blower? No way!' — Angel justifies it via the convincing kiss
jokes.setup: Danny is surprised Eve might be with Blower
jokes.punchline: Angel's evidence is that 'their kiss was the only convincing moment' in three hours of acting — using theatrical analysis as grounds for a police inference about infidelity
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Angel's evidence-based thinking applied to social situations. His calm deduction about an affair from am-dram acting quality is both funny and characterizes him perfectly.

jokes.text: 'Marcus Carter's big brother said he'd fingered her up the duck pond.'
jokes.setup: Angel has just made a sober detective inference about Eve's romantic preferences; Danny claims to have his own intelligence
jokes.punchline: Danny's 'intelligence' is schoolyard gossip about fingering by the duck pond — the contrast with Angel's sophisticated deduction is total and perfectly character-specific
jokes.explanation: Perfect character contrast. Angel's detective logic → Danny's playground gossip. The specificity of 'up the duck pond' (a location) and the double meaning of 'fingered' (police slang vs. the obvious) makes this land hard. Very Danny — his adult emotional intelligence is frozen at approximately age 14.

jokes.text: Danny: 'You know that's the bloke we done for speeding earlier.' — confirming what the audience already knew
jokes.setup: Angel has had his 'Drive safe' horror moment
jokes.punchline: Danny helpfully states the obvious — confirming the callback Angel has already processed — with complete guilelessness
jokes.explanation: Functional button. Danny being one beat behind the audience (and Angel) is a character trait but the joke itself is fairly light. It lands mainly as a straight-man reaction.

jokes.text: Angel: 'Yeah. Hopefully, that's the last we'll see of him.' — immediately before the cut to Blower dying
jokes.setup: Angel makes a casual parting remark about Blower
jokes.punchline: The line is immediately followed by a scene where Blower is killed in a car crash — 'the last we'll see of him' becomes horrifyingly literal within seconds
jokes.explanation: Classic Wright dramatic irony executed with absolute precision. The cut from 'that's the last we'll see of him' to Blower's death scene is one of the film's best structural jokes — comedic foreshadowing that becomes black comedy within a single edit. High rewatch bonus because on second viewing you're waiting for it. The economy of the line ('the last we'll see of him') in service of such a large payoff is exceptional.

jokes.text: 'I've had my top off in this lay-by.' / 'Tits.'
jokes.setup: Officers are examining the crash scene; one remarks that the car 'must have hit the sign at some speed. Took the whole top off.'
jokes.punchline: 'I've had my top off in this lay-by' — an officer's completely irrelevant personal confession — responded to with 'Tits.' — which is simultaneously an obscene exclamation and a descriptor of the irrelevant revelation
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy. The double meaning of 'took the whole top off' (the car roof/someone's shirt) is set up wordlessly; 'I've had my top off in this lay-by' implies a romantic/exhibitionist past; 'Tits.' is both a one-word dismissal and the literal implication. Three levels of meaning in four words total. Classic Wright verbal efficiency.

jokes.text: Angel: 'Constable, official vocab guidelines state we no longer refer to these incidents as "accidents," they're now "collisions."'
jokes.setup: Danny calls the crash a 'car accident'; Angel immediately corrects him with an official vocabulary guideline
jokes.punchline: In the middle of a death scene, Angel deploys procedural pedantry about terminology — the bureaucratic reflex at maximum inappropriate timing
jokes.explanation: Good character-comedy. Angel's procedural pedantry at a death scene is both funny and an important character moment — he processes everything through protocol. The word choice ('collisions') is also thematically resonant: 'accident' implies no blame, 'collision' implies causation — which matters for what follows.

jokes.text: 'For never was there a story of more woe. Than this of Juliet and her Romeo.' — Butterman quotes Shakespeare at the crash scene
jokes.setup: Officers are standing at the crash scene of two people who were just at a Romeo and Juliet performance
jokes.punchline: Butterman's Shakespeare quote — the final lines of Romeo and Juliet — applied to the actual deaths of people who just performed the play is blackly comic, especially since they were having an affair
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant dark comedy. The circle from performance to real death is complete, and Butterman quoting the play's final lines over real bodies is both funny and chilling.
