It also quietly implicates Butterman — did he know? The rewatch bonus is significant. The callback to the performance makes this land harder than it would as a standalone joke.

jokes.text: "Mr. Skinner, do you mind telling me how you know the identity of the persons involved?" / "You know how it is. News travels fast."
jokes.setup: Skinner quotes Shakespeare and refers to the victims by name, but their identities haven't been officially released.
jokes.punchline: Skinner's breezy 'news travels fast' is the most suspicious possible response — delivered with his characteristic pleasant menace — which is funny precisely because it's such an obvious tell that everyone around him ignores.
jokes.explanation: Good plotting-as-comedy moment. The joke is that Skinner's alibi is hilariously thin and Angel clocks it immediately while everyone else is oblivious. Character integration is high for Skinner — his self-satisfaction is palpable.

jokes.text: Danny explains why 'accident' is no longer used: 'Because "accident" implies there's nobody to blame.' / Officer: 'Put a sock in it, town mouse.'
jokes.setup: Danny tries to explain Angel's vocabulary correction to the other officers, apparently having just learned it
jokes.punchline: 'Put a sock in it, town mouse' — the other officer dismisses the vocabulary lesson with contempt, resenting Angel's London-cop superior attitude even when relayed by Danny
jokes.explanation: 'Town mouse' is a good insult for Angel delivered via Danny — the resentment of the village officers toward the London import plays well. The redirect of contempt to Danny (who agrees with Angel for once) has a nice irony.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, you wanna be a big cop in a small town, fuck off up the model village.'
jokes.setup: Angel is being dismissed by the village officers who don't want his London expertise
jokes.punchline: 'Fuck off up the model village' — 'model village' as an insult about Angel's big-cop-small-pond status is brilliantly specific to Sandford, which actually has a model village
jokes.explanation: Exceptional insult. 'Fuck off up the model village' works on three levels: it's a local geographic reference (Sandford has an actual model village), a size-based metaphor (Angel is a 'big cop' in a miniature world), and a genuinely funny dismissal. The specificity to this world is what elevates it above a generic insult. High quotability and genuine originality — this joke couldn't exist in any other film.

jokes.text: 'Jumping the Kalashnikov' — malapropism for 'jumping the gun'
jokes.setup: An officer accuses Angel of drawing premature conclusions about the crash
jokes.punchline: 'Jumping the Kalashnikov' instead of 'jumping the gun' — a malapropism that escalates the idiom from firearm to Soviet assault rifle
jokes.explanation: Smart malapropism. 'Kalashnikov' for 'gun' maintains the idiom's logic while making it absurdly specific. The character who says this is trying to sound authoritative while being fractionally wrong — a perfect one-beat character joke. 'Kalashnikov' as a word is funny in a way 'gun' is not.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, or put a call into Aaron A. Aaronson, shall we?' — sardonic suggestion about interviewing Blower's clients alphabetically
jokes.setup: Angel suggests interviewing Martin Blower's clients; an officer points out Blower represents most of the village
jokes.punchline: 'Aaron A. Aaronson' as the obviously alphabetically-first entry in a phone book is the hyperbolic conclusion to 'you'd have to go through the whole phone book'
jokes.explanation: Good comic hyperbole. 'Aaron A. Aaronson' as the archetypal phone-book first entry (triple-A for maximum alphabetical priority) is specific enough to be genuinely funny. The name itself is a mini-joke about people gaming alphabetical listings.

jokes.text: 'Skid marks.' / 'Now who's being childish?'
jokes.setup: Angel argues his case about the suspicious crash — he has forensic evidence
jokes.punchline: He announces 'Skid marks' (forensic evidence) but the word triggers a childish reaction; when it's pointed out, the officer calls him childish, but Angel was being entirely literal — the reversal lands on the officer
jokes.explanation: Classic double-meaning reversal. The officer accuses Angel of childishness for saying 'skid marks' — but Angel immediately demonstrates it's forensic evidence, turning the accusation back on the officer. The 'Now who's being childish?' callback is clean.

jokes.text: Butterman resolves the investigation standoff with: 'Well, a spot of bother up at Ellroy Farm. Old Arthur Webley's been clipping hedgerows that don't belong to him.' / 'That's it.'
jokes.setup: Angel has just made a compelling case that two people may have been murdered; Butterman shuts it down
jokes.punchline: 'That's it.' — Butterman's total dismissal of a potential homicide to attend a hedge-trimming dispute is the purest expression of Sandford's inverted priorities
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best structural jokes. Butterman's 'Old Arthur Webley's been clipping hedgerows that don't belong to him. That's it.' cuts Angel off mid-homicide-theory with a neighbourhood dispute. The perfect embodiment of Sandford's comedic inversion of priorities — hedge-related issues supersede murders. 'Yes, sir.' from Angel (enforced compliance) makes it complete.

jokes.text: 'Why do we need the dog?' / 'It's not the dog we need.'
jokes.setup: They are heading to deal with a hedge dispute; Danny questions why they need the police dog
jokes.punchline: 'It's not the dog we need' — immediately cutting to what they actually need (the dog's handler's ability to translate Old Webley, or the implied follow-up visual)
jokes.explanation: Good setup-and-reveal. The question of why the dog is needed misdirects — the dog is a vehicle for bringing the handler who can translate Webley's thick accent. Brief but effective.

jokes.text: The officer translates Old Webley's dialect: 'He said, "An 'edge is an 'edge. He only chopped it down 'cause it spoilt his view. What's Reaper moaning about?"'
jokes.setup: Webley speaks in such thick rural dialect that he requires translation; the dog handler serves as interpreter
jokes.punchline: The translated content is as banal as the dispute itself — 'An 'edge is an 'edge' — a philosophy of property rights reduced to rural tautology
jokes.explanation: 'An 'edge is an 'edge' is a genuinely funny rural-philosophical pronouncement. The translator device (needing a dog handler to translate another English speaker's English) is an excellent joke about Sandford's insularity and Angel's London outsider status. The hedgehog-philosophy logic of 'An 'edge is an 'edge' is quotable.

jokes.text: 'He does for this one. / What do you mean by "this one"?' — Webley's firearms collection begins to emerge
jokes.setup: Angel asks Webley about his firearm license; the officer confirms he has one
jokes.punchline: 'He does for this one' — implying there are more unlicensed weapons — the phrasing 'this one' opens a comedic abyss of unregistered firearms
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word setup ('this one') for the full escalating reveal. The horror implicit in 'this one' — establishing plurality — is excellent comic structure. Angel's slow 'What do you mean by "this one"?' response sells the dawning realization.

jokes.text: 'By the power of Grey Skull.' — Angel's reaction to seeing Webley's enormous secret weapons cache
jokes.setup: Webley opens what turns out to be a massive illegal arms cache in a rural farmhouse
jokes.punchline: Angel's involuntary He-Man reference — 'By the power of Grey Skull' — as a sincere expression of awe at the sight is a perfect culture-clash comic reaction
jokes.explanation: 'By the power of Grey Skull' is one of the reel's best single-line jokes. The He-Man reference as an involuntary exclamation is both perfectly specific (what other cultural touchstone conveys 'enormous shocking power'?) and funny precisely because it's not what a police sergeant should say. The fact that it's an earnest childhood-cartoon invocation rather than a deliberate joke makes it land harder. Very high quotability. The juxtaposition of a rural farmhouse arms cache with 1980s cartoon dialogue is classic Wright absurdism.

jokes.text: 'Where on earth did you get these?' / 'Found them.' / 'He found them!'
jokes.setup: Angel surveys a massive weapons cache including military hardware
jokes.punchline: Webley's explanation 'Found them' — delivered as if finding mortars and sea mines in a field is unremarkable — and the officer's echo 'He found them!' captures both the absurdity and the dark comedy perfectly
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy. 'Found them' as a complete explanation for a weapons arsenal is deadpan English rural logic at its finest. The echo 'He found them!' functions as the audience surrogate reaction — someone has to process this for us. The simplicity of the exchange makes it land hard.

jokes.text: 'And what is this?' / 'Sea mine.' — delivered flatly, amid a farm full of weapons
jokes.setup: Angel is cataloguing the increasingly insane weapons cache
jokes.punchline: 'Sea mine.' — Webley's matter-of-fact identification of a naval weapon found on an inland English farm
jokes.explanation: 'Sea mine' as a farmyard object delivered with zero affect is pitch-perfect absurdist deadpan. The word 'sea' is what makes it — it implies a vessel or ocean, not rural Gloucestershire. Each item in the cache is funnier because it's more improbable, and sea mine peaks the escalation.

jokes.text: 'No, apparently it's been deactivated.' / 'That's right, deactivated!' / 'It's not live.' / 'It looks live.'
jokes.setup: Officers have scattered from the sea mine in panic
jokes.punchline: Webley's belated 'it's deactivated' — delivered after the full evacuation — as though this was obvious information he could have shared earlier; 'It looks live' as Angel's lingering skepticism is the button
jokes.explanation: Good button on the sea mine sequence. Webley's 'Oh it's fine actually' after the scatter is a satisfying deflation of the slapstick panic. Angel's 'It looks live' maintains his wariness and is the right note to end on.

jokes.text: Unless you gotta water your Peace Lily.
jokes.setup: Angel has been established as a workaholic who refuses to socialize; Danny invites him to celebrate.
jokes.punchline: Danny pre-empts Angel's excuse with hyper-specific knowledge of his plant-watering habits, gently mocking his lonely routine.
jokes.explanation: Works because it's so oddly specific — 'Peace Lily' is a strange enough plant to be funny on its own, and Danny knowing Angel's routine implies a sweet surveillance-like attentiveness. Sets up the Peace Lily as a recurring motif. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Mr. Porter, what's your wine selection? / Oh, we got red or white.
jokes.setup: Angel asks a formal sommelier-style question about wine selection in a small village pub.
jokes.punchline: The barman's answer is the bluntest possible reduction of all wine to two colours.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical. The comedy is entirely in the gap between Angel's city-sophisticate register and the village pub's binary reality. The barman's total sincerity elevates it. Near-perfect structure for a single-beat gag.

jokes.text: And what can I get you that isn't a cranberry juice?
jokes.setup: Angel is known to abstain from alcohol; Danny orders for himself.
jokes.punchline: Danny pre-emptively rules out Angel's known non-alcoholic order, pushing him toward a real drink.
jokes.explanation: Solid character-based gag. The specificity of 'cranberry juice' as Angel's signature teetotal drink is a nice detail. Danny's gentle peer pressure is endearing and funny.

jokes.text: You don't switch off, do you? / You sound like my ex.
jokes.setup: Danny observes that Angel can't stop thinking about police work even at the pub.
jokes.punchline: Angel's reflexive comparison to his ex-girlfriend — delivered flatly — reveals his relational dysfunction as a running theme.
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat. The joke is mild — it's more character exposition than comedy — but the deadpan delivery and the implication that he's heard this before many times gives it a low-key charm.

jokes.text: What made you wanna be a policeman? / Officer. / What made you wanna be a policeman-officer?
jokes.setup: Angel corrects Danny's use of 'policeman' (the preferred term is 'police officer').
jokes.punchline: Danny obligingly fuses both terms into the absurd compound 'policeman-officer', achieving perfect grammatical compliance while defeating its purpose entirely.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever. Danny's literal-minded compliance produces an oxymoronic portmanteau that is both linguistically absurd and perfectly in character for someone eager to please but not quite sharp enough. The beat is tight and the word itself ('policeman-officer') is inherently funny to say. Strong character integration — only Danny would solve it this way.

jokes.text: Apart from the summer of 1979 when I wanted to be Kermit the Frog.
jokes.setup: Angel delivers a sincere, earnest speech about always wanting to be a police officer.
jokes.punchline: The immediate qualifier undercuts the grand statement with a ridiculous childhood exception — Kermit the Frog.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection. The setup builds sincere earnestness, so the specificity of 'Kermit the Frog' and '1979' is perfectly calibrated — odd enough to be funny, specific enough to feel real. The year grounds it and prevents it from being merely random. Good comic economy.

jokes.text: Actually, he was arrested for selling drugs to students. / What a cunt.
jokes.setup: Angel describes Uncle Derek as the heroic inspiration for his entire career; Danny responds warmly 'He sounds like a good bloke.'
jokes.punchline: Angel reveals Derek was a drug dealer; Danny's response is an utterly flat, perfectly timed obscenity — the most honest possible reaction.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the brutal simplicity of Danny's response. After a touching, earnest build-up, 'What a cunt' lands as the most honest, unfiltered reaction possible — and in one word says everything. The obscenity is not gratuitous; it's the exact right word delivered with perfect deadpan sincerity by Danny. High quotability. Classic British comedy register.

jokes.text: Probably bought the pedal car with the proceeds.
jokes.setup: Uncle Derek has just been revealed as a drug dealer; the beloved childhood pedal car now has a sinister origin.
jokes.punchline: Angel matter-of-factly connects the drug money to the pedal car, retroactively tainting his most cherished childhood memory.
jokes.explanation: Extends the drug dealer reveal with a darker implication — the symbol of Angel's moral awakening was funded by crime. The irony is well-constructed and adds a layer to his character. Earns the dark laugh through narrative logic rather than shock.

jokes.text: I think you would've made a great muppet.
jokes.setup: Angel has just delivered a passionate, moving speech about destiny and police work.
jokes.punchline: Danny returns to the Kermit aside and sincerely mourns the loss of a potential muppet career — undercutting the entire emotional speech.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. Angel's moving, sincere speech about his destiny builds considerable emotional weight, and Danny's chosen response — ignoring all of it to return sincerely to the Kermit detail — is perfect character comedy. It tells us everything about Danny (sweet, literal, slightly dim) while generating a big laugh through deflation. The sincerity of 'great muppet' is the key — he genuinely means it as a compliment.

jokes.text: Traffic collision. / I'm sorry. / Never mind. Hey, watch this.
jokes.setup: Angel asks sensitively how Danny's mother died; Danny answers flatly.
jokes.punchline: The briefest possible mourning period ('Never mind') followed by an immediate pivot to a party trick — Danny's emotional processing is devastatingly quick.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the whiplash speed of emotional processing. Danny answers honestly, accepts sympathy for approximately one second, then moves on. It's character-perfect — not played for laughs cruelly, but Danny's breezy relationship with grief is funny and endearing. The 'Never mind' is the key beat.

jokes.text: Danny does a bar trick that goes wrong — 'Jesus Christ! / Oh, my eye!'
jokes.setup: Danny tries to show off a trick at the bar to lighten the mood after the dead-mum revelation.
jokes.punchline: The trick goes catastrophically wrong, injuring someone (implied) and Danny's triumphant 'Ta-da!' follows regardless.
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy beat. The 'Ta-da!' after causing injury is the real gag — Danny's oblivious pride regardless of consequence. Works better visually than on page; the implied slapstick plus the triumphant flourish is a solid laugh.

jokes.text: What say we drink to their demise? / Shouldn't that be 'drink to their memories'?
jokes.setup: Skinner is discussing the death of Martin and Eve with apparent sympathy.
jokes.punchline: His toast to 'their demise' instead of their memories is a Freudian slip of villainous proportions — Angel catches it immediately.
jokes.explanation: Operates on multiple levels: played as a mild social gaffe on the surface, but functions as dramatic irony for the audience who may suspect Skinner. The word 'demise' is specific enough to be funny as a slip-up and sinister enough to be a clue. Skinner's immediate recovery ('Of course. Cheers.') is perfectly played. Strong character integration — only Skinner would say this.

jokes.text: 'I'm all right!' / 'Little being the operative word.'
jokes.setup: A small man (Skinner's associate?) drunkenly declares he's all right before heading to the loo.
jokes.punchline: Angel mutters 'little being the operative word' as a double entendre about both his stature and the 'little boys' room.'
jokes.explanation: Decent wordplay — 'little boys' room' + literally small man. The double meaning is clear and clean. Not exceptional but efficiently executed.

jokes.text: I think somebody needs to go home. / I'm... I'm not that drunk, sir. / Not you. Him.
jokes.setup: Danny defensively protests he's not that drunk, assuming Angel is talking about him.
jokes.punchline: Angel clarifies he meant someone else — the small drunk man — leaving Danny looking foolish for self-incriminating.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection beat. Danny's defensive protest does the comedic work for Angel — he didn't have to accuse Danny, Danny accused himself. Well-timed and economical.

jokes.text: 'Hey, we did get a little drunk. Did you get it? 'Cause he's... He's little and he's drunk.'
jokes.setup: Angel makes the 'little drunk' joke; Danny needs to explain it to Angel.
jokes.punchline: Danny explains the joke with complete earnestness — the explanation is more self-defeating and funnier than the original quip.
jokes.explanation: Danny explaining his own joke is perfectly in character and funnier than the original. His laboured 'He's little AND he's drunk' breakdown shows his pride in the wordplay, which is endearing and comic.

jokes.text: It's hardly in keeping with the village's rustic aesthetic, is it?
jokes.setup: They are outside, apparently looking at something incongruous in the picturesque village (implied neon sign or modern storefront).
jokes.punchline: Angel's dry observation about aesthetic incongruity in a situation that probably calls for a more practical concern.
jokes.explanation: Mild observational beat. Works as a character note — Angel's precision even in casual conversation. Not especially funny on the page; depends heavily on what is being observed visually.

jokes.text: Unless you wanna come in for a cup of coffee? / I don't drink coffee. / Tea? / No caffeine after midday. / How about another beer?
jokes.setup: Danny tries to extend the evening and invite Angel in; Angel declines each offer on hyper-specific health grounds.
jokes.punchline: The escalating rejections of increasingly mundane beverages make Angel seem impossibly rigid — until Danny offers the more serious option (beer) and Angel's hesitation is implied.
jokes.explanation: Nicely escalating exchange. Angel's fastidious rules about caffeine while beer remains acceptable is the ironic payoff — the alcoholic beverage bypasses all his health concerns. Good character work showing Angel's selective rigidity.

jokes.text: Janine used to say I love my Lily more than I loved her. / Is that why you split up? / 'Cause you did it with a plant?
jokes.setup: Angel explains his ex thought he was more attached to his Peace Lily than to her.
jokes.punchline: Danny interprets this as Angel having had a sexual relationship with the plant — a magnificently literal misunderstanding.
jokes.explanation: Danny's literal-minded leap to bestiality/plant-intercourse is absurd but perfectly in character — his mind goes places no one else would. The deadpan sincerity of the question sells it completely. Also a nice callback to the Peace Lily motif. High character integration.

jokes.text: I did miss a few dinners. You know, parties, a birthday or two. / Her dad's funeral.
jokes.setup: Angel lists the minor social events he missed due to work obsession, building to a mild self-justification.
jokes.punchline: He casually adds 'Her dad's funeral' as if it's the same magnitude as a birthday — the escalation reveals a spectacular lack of self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: Classic Edgar Wright escalation. The list goes: dinners → parties → birthdays → HER DAD'S FUNERAL. The rhythm builds and the final item is a category error — lumped in casually with trivial things. The beat before it ('Listen, mate, I...') from Danny — an attempted intervention — makes the reveal funnier because we expect something mild. Well-structured dark comedy.

jokes.text: By the power of Grey Skull. Point Break or Bad Boys II?
jokes.setup: Danny promises to show Angel how to switch off; Angel sceptically asks what he has in mind.
jokes.punchline: Danny's 'By the power of Grey Skull' invocation (a He-Man reference) followed immediately by a choice between two 90s action movies is both absurd and perfectly character-defining.
jokes.explanation: The He-Man cry as a ceremonial incantation before presenting action film options is quintessentially Danny — a man whose entire emotional world is organised around pop culture. The specificity of Point Break and Bad Boys II (not just 'action films') is key. High character integration score.

jokes.text: Well, I won't argue that it was a no holds barred, adrenalin fuelled thrill ride but there's no way you could perpetrate that amount of carnage and mayhem and not incur a considerable amount of paperwork.
jokes.setup: Danny and Angel have watched Point Break (or Bad Boys II); Danny asks for Angel's reaction.
jokes.punchline: Angel's response is not about whether it was entertaining but about the procedural paperwork that would result from the action — his cop brain cannot be turned off even during leisure.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The language ('perpetrate...carnage and mayhem') is itself comedy — Angel reviewing an action film in the vocabulary of a police report. It directly pays off the 'can't switch off' thread from the whole pub sequence. The specificity of 'paperwork' as the film's flaw is both deeply in character and a sharply original critical stance. Highly quotable. This is the kind of joke that becomes a touchstone for the film.

jokes.text: That is nothing, man. This is about to go off.
jokes.setup: Angel critiques the first film; Danny dismisses it and promises the second will be even more over the top.
jokes.punchline: Danny is completely unbothered by Angel's procedural critique and doubles down — his dedication to mindless spectacle is total.
jokes.explanation: Light character beat extending the film-watching gag. Danny's total enthusiasm for escalating action is funny in context but not especially remarkable on its own.

jokes.text: This shit just got real.
jokes.setup: Danny is watching Bad Boys II and delivers the film's famous line with complete sincerity.
jokes.punchline: Danny quoting the film approvingly while Angel presumably sits in stone-faced silence — the meta-layer is that the audience knows this line too.
jokes.explanation: Works as a pop culture citation with character affection. Danny's reverence for the line is funny; the joke gets a later massive callback when it's said for real in the finale (not in this reel). Modest laugh here but significant setup value.

jokes.text: Nasty way to go. / I think our Mr. Merchant tried to have a little fry up and left the gas on.
jokes.setup: George Merchant's house has exploded and he is dead; officers survey the wreckage.
jokes.punchline: The cheerful domestic explanation ('little fry up') for a massive explosion casualty is delivered with total mundane calm — treating a violent death as kitchen negligence.
jokes.explanation: The cheerful domesticity of 'little fry up' against the backdrop of an explosion death is a nice dark-comedy register shift. 'Little' as a diminutive for a fatal gas explosion is quietly absurd.

jokes.text: Spends his whole life devoted to the refrigerator then gets killed by an oven.
jokes.setup: George Merchant, a self-made millionaire obsessed with his fancy home and possessions, has died in a kitchen explosion.
jokes.punchline: His life is summarised as a battle between appliances — devoted to fridge, killed by oven — a mordantly reductive eulogy.
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical dark comedy. The fridge/oven contrast is a clever structural inversion — the thing he loved (fridge/food/wealth) versus the thing that killed him (oven/fire). Works as an absurd life summary. Good economy — maximum comedy per word.

jokes.text: I told him several times, you shouldn't eat late at night. / Oh, I don't know. I quite like a little midnight gobble. / Cocks.
jokes.setup: Officers discuss Merchant's fatal late-night fry-up. Skinner makes a suggestive comment about 'midnight gobble.'
jokes.punchline: Angel's single-word response — 'Cocks.' — is delivered deadpan, apparently describing something in the rubble (cockerel ornaments?), but functions as an obscene exclamation responding to the double entendre.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy — one word doing triple duty: (1) Angel describing decorative cockerels in the rubble, (2) functioning as an expletive reaction to Skinner's innuendo, (3) the visual of Angel cataloguing debris while saying 'Cocks.' Edgar Wright's signature layered wordplay. Near-perfect economy score.

jokes.text: Actually, I just wanted to ask, 'What's your perfect Sunday?'
jokes.setup: Angel tries to manage the press at an active crime/explosion scene; Messenger approaches for 'a quick word.'
jokes.punchline: The 'quick word' is not about the explosion at all — it's a fluff lifestyle question for the village paper, completely incongruous at a death scene.
jokes.explanation: Good contextual absurdism. The gulf between the seriousness of the scene and 'What's your perfect Sunday?' is very funny. Establishes Messenger as a small-town journalist of heroic inconsequence.

jokes.text: Now, my perfect Sunday is a lovely long lie in...
jokes.setup: The Inspector is supposed to be taking the press away from the crime scene, but instead immediately answers the fluff question himself.
jokes.punchline: He enthusiastically describes his perfect Sunday at an explosion death scene — revealing his total commitment to village life over police work.
jokes.explanation: Nice character beat — the Inspector's priorities are hilariously wrong. By engaging with the lifestyle question he reveals his fundamental unseriousness as a police authority figure.

jokes.text: Something like, something out of Backdraft.
jokes.setup: Skinner is describing the fire/explosion with apparent distress for the cameras.
jokes.punchline: He cites the Ron Howard firefighting drama as his reference point for the explosion — revealing that his emotional responses are entirely film-mediated, just like Danny's.
jokes.explanation: Mild character note. Skinner reaching for a film comparison at a death scene is slightly suspicious and slightly funny — not a major beat but adds texture.

jokes.text: Namely a Sergeant Knickerless Asswipe and a Constable Fanny Batterbum.
jokes.setup: Fisher formally identifies the last people to see Merchant alive; the audience expects police formality.
jokes.punchline: He reads out absurd malapropisms of Angel's and Danny's names (Nicholas Angel → Knickerless Asswipe; Danny Butterman → Fanny Batterbum) with complete official seriousness.
jokes.explanation: Juvenile wordplay delivered with procedural gravitas is always funny. 'Knickerless Asswipe' is an admirably committed mangling. The official-document register amplifies the silliness. Broad but executed well.

jokes.text: That's us. / Why is this such a big joke to you? Three people have died in a week.
jokes.setup: Danny cheerfully identifies them from the rude name mangling; Angel's frustration is genuine.
jokes.punchline: Angel's exasperated call-out — 'Why is this such a big joke to you?' — is itself funny because the answer is obvious: because it IS a joke. Angel's straight-man sincerity is the comedy.
jokes.explanation: Angel as frustrated straight man. The irony of him asking why something is a joke, in a comedy, is mild meta-humour. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: It's a bit of a blind spot, I'm afraid. We just catch the very edge of the explosion.
jokes.setup: Angel asks who might have seen something suspicious; the Neighborhood Watch is consulted.
jokes.punchline: The Neighborhood Watch, whose entire purpose is surveillance, has a 'blind spot' that conveniently missed an explosion — the defining irony of useless officious surveillance.
jokes.explanation: Nice ironic beat — Neighborhood Watch failing at watching. Understated and in keeping with the film's slow-burn satirical approach to village life.

jokes.text: Sandford's most wanted. There you go. It was the swan all along.
jokes.setup: Angel reviews CCTV footage hoping for a lead on the deaths; instead sees the escaped swan.
jokes.punchline: Fisher sarcastically proposes the swan as the murder suspect — a callback to the earlier chase and implied running gag about the swan being the village's biggest problem.
jokes.explanation: Running gag payoff. The swan as Sandford's most wanted criminal is absurd and consistent with the village's distorted priorities. Gets a decent laugh from accumulated context. The rewatch value is in knowing the swan's eventual significance.

jokes.text: Oh, give over, Miss Marples. / Yeah, you do your job and we'll do ours, eh? / Yeah. Haven't you got a church fete to look after? / No, I have not! / Actually.
jokes.setup: Doctor Hatcher is frustrated that police aren't taking the deaths seriously; the officers dismiss her with condescending pop culture references.
jokes.punchline: The 'Actually' — presumably from someone else confirming she does have a church fete to look after — perfectly caps the dismissal and deflates her righteous indignation.
jokes.explanation: The 'Actually' is the entire joke — a one-word confirmation that completely destroys her dignity. The structure is well-built: condescension → righteous denial → confirmed anyway. Tight.

jokes.text: Shark!
jokes.setup: The village fete is underway; a child is playing a game (possibly 'splat the rat' mentioned nearby).
jokes.punchline: A child shouts 'Shark!' — presumably at something that is emphatically not a shark — in an entirely landlocked village fete context.
jokes.explanation: Brief absurdist non-sequitur. Very short, low context. The incongruity of 'Shark' at a village fete gets a mild laugh but is too thin to rank highly.

jokes.text: Seen any murderings, Nicholarse?
jokes.setup: Local kids have been teasing Angel about murder since earlier reels.
jokes.punchline: The deliberate mispronunciation 'Nicholarse' (Nicholas + arse) maintains the kids' cheerful disrespect while referencing the murder investigation as idle entertainment.
jokes.explanation: 'Nicholarse' is a juvenile but efficiently rude name-twist. Functions as running gag maintenance. Not exceptional but consistent.

jokes.text: Three cans wins you the squeaky bunny, five cans gets you the floppy lion. Take out all the little people, you get to waltz off with the cuddly monkey.
jokes.setup: It's an air rifle stall at the fete; prizes are described in ascending order.
jokes.punchline: The final prize — 'waltz off with the cuddly monkey' — is set up as special, and 'take out all the little people' has a slightly sinister ring, but the real payoff is that Angel (a firearms expert) is about to annihilate the stall.
jokes.explanation: Setup joke — the real punchline comes at 54:25 when Angel devastates the range. The escalating prize list with the goofy toy names is moderately amusing on its own and sets up the visual payoff well.

jokes.text: I thought I made it clear to you how I feel about firearms. / It's only an air rifle.
jokes.setup: Angel has established strict anti-firearms principles; Danny presents an air rifle at a fete.
jokes.punchline: Danny's 'it's only an air rifle' minimises Angel's principled objection to guns with the most childlike possible counterargument.
jokes.explanation: Setup beat for the visual payoff. Mild on its own but serves its structural purpose perfectly.

jokes.text: Dear Lord! That was amazing. [Angel obliterates the entire rifle range with perfect marksmanship]
jokes.setup: Angel has declared anti-firearms principles but reluctantly takes the air rifle; the stall operator says 'Sergeant' — implying Angel's reputation precedes him.
jokes.punchline: Angel proceeds to destroy every target with terrifying precision, earning 'Dear Lord! That was amazing.' — his firearms expertise making a mockery of his stated principles.
jokes.explanation: Superb payoff to Angel's firearms principle. The joke works on character irony: his insistence on not liking guns is immediately demolished by his incredible competence with them. The escalation from reluctance to devastating accuracy is classic Edgar Wright — the action speaks louder. The stall operator's 'Dear Lord' is the perfect reaction. Comparable in construction quality to the film's best set-pieces.

jokes.text: I can't believe I shot someone. / He's a doctor, he can deal with it.
jokes.setup: In the chaos of Angel's shooting display, Danny has apparently accidentally shot someone with the air rifle.
jokes.punchline: Angel's completely unfazed response — 'He's a doctor, he can deal with it' — treats accidental shooting as a minor admin issue.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark beat. Angel's breezy dismissal — 'He's a doctor, he can deal with it' — is both logistically sensible and completely callous. The logic is impeccable, which makes it funnier. Good economy.

jokes.text: Danny, believe me, it's not something you ever get used to.
jokes.setup: Danny says he's never shot anyone before; Angel responds gravely.
jokes.punchline: Angel's earnest 'it's not something you ever get used to' — delivered with the gravity of a war veteran — is about an air rifle pellet at a village fete.
jokes.explanation: Nice tonal incongruity. The veteran-cop gravitas applied to a fairground air rifle injury is funny. Also plants a seed for the action climax — it's a preview of how seriously they'll eventually take gunfighting.

jokes.text: Service. [correcting the MC who said 'Force']
jokes.setup: The MC announces Angel as a member of the 'Sandford Police Force.'
jokes.punchline: Angel's reflexive one-word correction — 'Service' — interrupts the introduction, maintaining his pedantic consistency about terminology.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one word does all the work. The running gag is well-worn by now, so it's not a big laugh, but the context (interrupting a public announcement) makes it slightly funnier than usual. Character consistency at maximum efficiency.

jokes.text: Prick. / Wanker. [muttered by villagers as Angel takes the stage]
jokes.setup: Angel is being announced as a celebrated addition to the village; the crowd applauds.
jokes.punchline: Two villagers quietly mutter 'Prick' and 'Wanker' — the gap between official celebration and actual sentiment.
jokes.explanation: Good subversive beat. The juxtaposition of official celebration with muttered contempt is funny and hints at the village's darker relationship with Angel. On rewatch, knowing the villagers are literally a murderous conspiracy, it lands differently.

jokes.text: The first name is Simon Skinner. [pause] He's in the loo. / Too much of Joyce's lemonade, perhaps.
jokes.setup: Angel draws the raffle; the first winner is Skinner — a moment of mild tension/dramatic irony.
jokes.punchline: He's in the loo. The Inspector's jovial domestic explanation deflates any tension completely.
jokes.explanation: Mild beat — the domestic specificity of 'Joyce's lemonade' in an official context is quietly funny. The 'Too much of Joyce's lemonade' has charming village-gossip warmth.

jokes.text: Tim, your number's up.
jokes.setup: Angel draws the next raffle number and announces the winner — Tim Messenger.
jokes.punchline: The phrase 'your number's up' is a death idiom — Angel unknowingly delivers a death sentence in the same breath as a raffle prize announcement. Tim is about to be killed.
jokes.explanation: Perfect dark dramatic irony. The audience may not catch it on first view, but on rewatch — knowing Tim is seconds from death — 'your number's up' is exquisitely cruel and funny. Classic Edgar Wright layered scripting. The innocence of the raffle context against the idiomatic death meaning is sharp. High rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Who could do something like this? / Maybe it was the swan. / Apparently, they can break a man's arm. / Or blow up a man's house.
jokes.setup: Tim Messenger has just been killed; Angel is horrified; the officers riff on swan capabilities.
jokes.punchline: The officers escalate their swan theory to include arson — continuing the absurd running gag at maximally inappropriate timing.
jokes.explanation: Running gag escalation at a genuinely dark moment — Tim has just died horribly. The officers returning to the swan theory is both funny and revealing of their total incompetence/complicity. The escalation to arson ('blow up a man's house') is a good beat.

jokes.text: Oh, he's got shorts on.
jokes.setup: Officers are being urgently deployed to investigate a murder scene at the church fete.
jokes.punchline: Fisher's observation about a colleague's shorts — delivered in the same serious tone as the deployment orders — is a staggeringly irrelevant detail.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant non-sequitur deadpan. During a murder deployment, Fisher's irrelevant uniform observation — delivered with equal gravity — is perfectly absurdist. The gap between the seriousness of the moment and the triviality of the observation is very funny.

jokes.text: I was extremely shocked when I looked at my watch and discovered that I should be in the pub.
jokes.setup: Angel asks if Fisher found anything investigating the murder scene.
jokes.punchline: Fisher's 'discovery' is entirely about pub opening hours — his investigation yielded nothing but awareness of when he should be drinking.
jokes.explanation: Very well constructed. 'Extremely shocked when I looked at my watch and discovered' builds expectation of a genuine revelation; the punchline is perfectly bathetic. The language ('extremely shocked') is delightfully overblown for such a trivial discovery. Fisher character defined efficiently.

jokes.text: Did you go to his house? Did you read his articles? / If you wanna wade through every copy of the Sandford bloody Citizen, be our guest. / It's your job, isn't it? Detect!
jokes.setup: Angel asks Fisher if he investigated the murder properly.
jokes.punchline: Fisher passes off basic police detective work onto Angel with 'be our guest' — and Angel's exasperated one-word comeback 'Detect!' is both a reasonable demand and very funny in its simplicity.
jokes.explanation: Angel's 'Detect!' is the punch — a frustrated reduction of an entire job to one imperative verb. Fisher's blithe dismissal of detective work is consistent characterisation.

jokes.text: It's high time you realized that. You and your monkey.
jokes.setup: Fisher dismisses Angel's murder theory and exits, but then looks at or references the giant stuffed monkey Angel won at the rifle range.
jokes.punchline: 'You and your monkey' — Fisher includes the stuffed toy as Angel's equal partner in his investigation.
jokes.explanation: Nice callback to the rifle range. The stuffed monkey as Angel's detective partner is absurd and slightly deflating. The image of Angel clutching a giant toy while earnestly discussing murder is funny.

jokes.text: Did he mean me or that? [Angel gesturing at the stuffed monkey]
jokes.setup: Fisher has insulted Angel and his monkey as a unit.
jokes.punchline: Danny genuinely cannot determine whether the insult was aimed at him or the stuffed toy — revealing that he may consider himself on par with a fairground prize.
jokes.explanation: Danny's oblivious self-comparison to a stuffed animal is characteristically dim and endearing. The beat works because of its sincerity — he's not making a joke, he genuinely doesn't know. Perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: You said I could be an amazing policeman-officer. / There's always something going on, Danny.
jokes.setup: Angel tries to motivate Danny; Danny claims to remember something Angel said.
jokes.punchline: Danny's callback is to the 'policeman-officer' mangling from earlier — he has remembered the exact wrong thing with the exact wrong terminology, earnestly.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. Danny has absorbed exactly the wrong lesson — he's held onto the corrected terminology as if it's Angel's greatest wisdom, deploying 'policeman-officer' again with pride. Perfectly in character and structurally very satisfying as a callback. Shows both his admiration for Angel and his literal-mindedness.

jokes.text: You don't know how to switch off! [Danny chases Angel with this point, then Angel reads the Sandford Citizen all night]
jokes.setup: Angel told Danny the whole evening that he can't switch off; Danny tries to use this against him.
jokes.punchline: Danny now deploying Angel's own self-criticism back at him — but it backfires because Angel immediately switches to reading the Citizen all night, proving Danny correct.
jokes.explanation: Good structural callback — Danny using Angel's vulnerability against him, only for Angel to immediately validate the critique by diving straight into work. The comic beat is in Angel's inability to stop even when directly confronted with the problem.

jokes.text: Angel, alone at night, reads through every issue of the Sandford Citizen spread across Danny's floor, surrounded by evidence — the visual of a cop going full conspiracy-board
jokes.setup: Angel was told sarcastically to 'wade through every copy of the Sandford bloody Citizen' if he wanted answers
jokes.punchline: He literally does exactly that — the visual of a meticulous cop treating a sleepy village newspaper archive as a murder investigation is both funny and characterizing
jokes.explanation: Visual callback gag. The literalism of Angel taking the sarcastic suggestion seriously is good character comedy. Edgar Wright would score and edit this as a parody of the classic detective-research montage.

jokes.text: Thanks for the monkey. / Yours, isn't it? / I won it for you.
jokes.setup: Morning after. Danny acknowledges the stuffed monkey.
jokes.punchline: Angel deflects ownership; Danny insists he won it specifically for Angel — a sweet, slightly absurd gift from one man to another of a giant fairground monkey.
jokes.explanation: Mild but warm character beat. The stuffed monkey as an intentional gift reveals Danny's affection for Angel. Modest laugh but good for relationship building.

jokes.text: We? / Come on, partner. Let's go to work.
jokes.setup: Angel announces he's figured out a connection; Danny offers to help.
jokes.punchline: Angel's surprised 'We?' followed by his accepting 'Come on, partner' is a small but warm comedic beat — Angel accepting Danny as a genuine equal for the first time.
jokes.explanation: More of a character/emotional beat than a pure comedy moment. The 'We?' registers as a surprised laugh, then 'partner' lands warmly. Pleasant but not especially funny.

jokes.text: The rapid-fire detective duet — 'Fondness for puns / Go on. Terrible speller / Oh yeah? Nevertheless had uncovered important information about... George Merchant. Self-made millionaire...' etc.
jokes.setup: Angel and Danny work through the connections between the victims in a stylised back-and-forth.
jokes.punchline: The sequence escalates with Danny contributing absurd but accurate details ('Pissed on the floor in The Crown') alongside serious ones, culminating in 'Favored older men / Fingered' — Danny's characteristically blunt summation.
jokes.explanation: One of the best sequences in the reel. The rapid-fire detective ping-pong is an Edgar Wright stylistic signature — maximum information at maximum speed. The comedy comes from the rhythm, the juxtaposition of serious leads ('solicitor', 'planning and development') with Danny's blunt pop-culture-speak ('pissed on the floor', 'Fingered', 'Affirmatron'). The structure is impeccable. 'Affirmatron' as Danny's affirmative response is a minor gem. 'Fingered' as a succinct summary of an affair is perfectly Danny. This sequence is film-defining in terms of style and character.

jokes.text: So... maybe they were all accidents. People have accidents every day.
jokes.setup: Angel and Danny have just painstakingly constructed a conspiracy connecting all three deaths.
jokes.punchline: After the entire brilliant detective duet, Danny deflates it completely by echoing the police's earlier dismissive line back as if he's considered it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural beat. The elaborate detective sequence builds to what feels like a genuine revelation, then Danny pulls the rug by citing the police's idiotic dismissal — as if all that work might have led nowhere. It's funny because it's both a callback and a character reveal (Danny can hold two contradictory things with equal weight). The timing is impeccable. Angel's reaction must be priceless.

jokes.text: Danny, why didn't you say something? / We were working, weren't we?
jokes.setup: It's Angel's birthday and no one mentioned it; a surprise is revealed.
jokes.punchline: Danny's defence — 'We were working, weren't we?' — echoes Angel's own work-obsession back at him; for once Danny prioritised police business over socialising.
jokes.explanation: Nice role-reversal payoff. Danny deploying Angel's own work-first logic is touching and funny — especially since Danny presumably knew all day and suppressed his natural enthusiasm. Well-integrated callback.

jokes.text: Well, George Merchant, God rest him...Martin Blower, God rest him...Eve Draper, God rest her...that reporter, God rest him...[continuing accumulation of 'God rest him/her']
jokes.setup: Miss Tiller explains the property deal; she mentions each recently deceased person.
jokes.punchline: Every single dead person gets their own 'God rest him/her' — the formula repeating with mechanical regularity becomes funnier with each repetition, culminating in 'God rest the lot of them.'
jokes.explanation: Classic escalating running gag. Miss Tiller's reflexive piety about each corpse — applied indiscriminately to all the murder victims she's inadvertently naming — becomes funnier each time. 'God rest the lot of them' is a perfect summation. The comedy is in the formula's relentlessness and her complete unawareness that she's narrating a conspiracy. Edgar Wright's comedic escalation at its finest in this sequence.

jokes.text: as far as I'm concerned, Cousin Sissy can go and fuck— / Would you just excuse me, for just one second?
jokes.setup: Miss Tiller is wrapping up her property explanation with mild domestic drama about Cousin Sissy.
jokes.punchline: She's about to deliver an emphatic obscenity — Angel cuts her off mid-word to presumably pursue a lead, leaving 'fuck—' hanging.
jokes.explanation: Nice beat — the genteel old lady about to drop a magnificent obscenity, interrupted at the worst/best possible moment. The structure is clean: build sweet old lady register → subvert with vulgarity mid-word → cut away. The 'for just one second' politeness while abandoning her sentence is very funny.

jokes.text: Stop! In the name of the law!
jokes.setup: Angel pursues a suspect (presumably the killer fleeing after the Miss Tiller information).
jokes.punchline: Angel yelling the most clichéd cop-movie command possible — perfectly sincere, completely ridiculous in a small English village — is both genre parody and character comedy.
jokes.explanation: The reel ends on this broad action-movie parody line. It's a reasonable button — Angel finally acting like the action hero he's been restrained from being — but the line itself is stock. Gets a laugh from context more than writing.

jokes.text: The rapid-fire confirmation of murders — 'What, just like Tim Messenger?' 'Yes!' / 'And George Merchant?' 'Yes!' / 'And Eve Draper?' 'Yes!' / 'And Martin Blower?' 'No, actually.' / 'Really?' / ''Course he fucking was!'
jokes.setup: Angel is confirming each murder victim in a building rhythm, the audience expects the same 'Yes!' for every name
jokes.punchline: He pauses on Martin Blower to say 'No, actually' — then immediately corrects himself with ''Course he fucking was!' — subverting the rhythm twice in quick succession
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in comedic rhythm disruption. The list-with-a-break structure is a classic comedy construction, but the double-beat — the false pause followed by the immediate self-correction — adds an extra layer. The profanity lands because it's not gratuitous; it's the character's exasperation breaking through. The structure alone earns this an 8+.

jokes.text: Andy dismisses a string of murders: 'Oh, murder, murder, murder. Change the fucking record.'
jokes.setup: Angel has just presented compelling evidence of multiple homicides
jokes.punchline: Andy treats it like a tired recurring complaint rather than a serious criminal matter — using a mundane idiom ('change the record') about murder
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of the gravity of murder with the casual domestic phrase 'change the fucking record' is sharp and highly quotable. Character-specific for the blunt, obstructive Sandford cops. Economy is excellent — six words do enormous comedic work.

jokes.text: 'What are you suggesting? That Leslie Tiller tripped and fell on her own shears?' / 'Ben Fletcher fell on his pitchfork the other week.'
jokes.setup: Angel poses the absurd scenario sarcastically — that Leslie tripped on her own shears — to demonstrate it's obviously a murder
jokes.punchline: The respondent completely misses the sarcasm and offers another absurd gardening-implement accident as a straight counterpoint
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the absurdist specificity of 'pitchfork' as a parallel, and the deadpan straight-faced delivery suggesting this person genuinely sees no problem. Reinforces the village's collective denial while getting a laugh.

jokes.text: 'What absolute horseshit.'
jokes.setup: Angel explains he was buying Danny a Japanese Peace Lily for his birthday — a surprisingly tender reason to be at a murder scene.
jokes.punchline: His own immediate self-contradiction: he delivers 'What absolute horseshit' as if objecting to someone else's explanation, when he was the one who just said the implausible thing. (Or alternatively, someone off-screen mutters it and Angel hears it.)
jokes.explanation: Ambiguous attribution makes this land oddly but it's a solid beat. The Peace Lily as evidence of Angel's genuine friendship with Danny is funny enough on its own; the 'horseshit' adds a coda of self-awareness.

jokes.text: 'Here, maybe it was our old friend, the cactus thief.' / 'Oh, yeah, he was a prickly customer, weren't he?'
jokes.setup: The Andys deflect the murder discussion by invoking the cactus theft — a minor crime that dominated their attention in earlier reels
jokes.punchline: 'Prickly customer' is a pun on cactus spines and also idiom for a difficult person — the Andys are pleased with themselves for this deflection
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that earns its laugh through the absurdity of invoking the cactus thief in the middle of a murder discussion — and the pun is groan-worthy in the best way. The character-specificity of the smug Andys makes it land.

jokes.text: 'Am I going completely mad?'
jokes.setup: Angel has just presented solid evidence of murder and everyone around him is dismissing it with cactus jokes
jokes.punchline: His genuine, exasperated rhetorical question — delivered as a sincere plea — is the punch. The audience knows he's right; everyone else is delusional.
jokes.explanation: A functional straight-man reaction beat that lets the audience align with Angel's frustration. The irony is clear and well-earned. Not exceptional, but lands solidly.

jokes.text: Response to 'Am I going completely mad?' — 'Maybe you are.'
jokes.setup: Angel asks a rhetorical question expecting reassurance or engagement
jokes.punchline: Frank gives a completely flat, earnest-seeming 'Maybe you are' — which on rewatch is sinister and knowing
jokes.explanation: Two words, devastating on rewatch. At first viewing it reads as dismissive humour; with knowledge of the third act it's Frank taunting Angel right to his face. The rewatch_bonus is high. Economy score is perfect — it cannot be shorter.

jokes.text: 'Maybe you did it. Yeah, seeing as how you're such a big fan of murder.'
jokes.setup: Angel is trying to be taken seriously about murders
jokes.punchline: The Andys accuse him of being the murderer because he's been talking about murder so much — absurd non-logic delivered as genuine reasoning
jokes.explanation: The absurdist logic ('fan of murder') played completely straight is very effective. It's funny precisely because it has the shape of logic without any actual logic. Character-specific to the obstructionist Andys.

jokes.text: 'The boys here aren't used to the concepts you're bandying about.'
jokes.setup: Frank is talking about murder investigations as if they're exotic academic ideas rather than standard policing
jokes.punchline: Calling 'murder' a 'concept' the boys aren't used to is an absurd euphemism that reveals the entire station's willful ignorance
jokes.explanation: Solid piece of characterisation comedy — the idea that murder is too advanced a 'concept' for Sandford cops is funny and reveals the villagers' constructed reality. Works better on rewatch when you know Frank is directing this.

jokes.text: 'The M word, Nicholas.'
jokes.setup: Frank has been dancing around calling the crimes 'murder'
jokes.punchline: He calls it 'the M word' as if it's a profanity too shocking to say aloud — treating murder like a social taboo rather than a police matter
jokes.explanation: Very economical and highly character-specific. The 'M word' construction inverts social convention — normally we avoid slurs, not police classifications. It encapsulates the entire village's pathology in three words. Strong quotability.

jokes.text: Skinner learns Leslie Tiller is dead and asks 'How?' — Angel responds 'She tripped and fell on her own shears' — the same thing the police told him.
jokes.setup: Earlier, the police dismissively told Angel that Leslie 'tripped and fell on her own shears'
jokes.punchline: Now Angel repeats the same line back flatly to the man he's accusing of the murder — it's simultaneously absurd and devastatingly ironic
jokes.explanation: A supremely crafted callback. Angel weaponizes the dismissive official line by deploying it to Skinner's face — it now reads as Angel's deadpan contempt for the cover story. The structure is perfect: same words, completely inverted meaning. Earns 8+ because the construction requires the full context of the film to land at maximum impact.

jokes.text: 'Very entertaining. But I rather think you've been watching too many films.'
jokes.setup: Angel has just delivered a cinematic detective monologue in a supermarket.
jokes.punchline: Skinner — IN a film — tells the character who just behaved like a movie detective that he's 'been watching too many films.' Pure meta self-reference.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. 'You've been watching too many films' — delivered to the protagonist of an action-movie parody, by the villain, in response to behavior that IS movie-cliché — is a layered piece of meta-comedy. It works on first watch as a dismissal and on rewatches as a wink. The fact that Angel's monologue was designed to parody detective genre conventions makes this the punchline to the entire scene. It's comparable to the 8.0 anchor and exceeds it slightly in originality.

jokes.text: Angel tries to embarrass Skinner with his nickname 'Cousin Sissy' — Skinner responds that it's 'only a revelation to yourself' and that his ballet studies are 'well known'
jokes.setup: Angel deploys 'Cousin Sissy' as a trump card, expecting it to embarrass Skinner
jokes.punchline: Skinner is completely unruffled — his teenage ballet and the nickname are openly known, making Angel look foolish for thinking it was a revelation
jokes.explanation: A satisfying subversion of the detective-reveals-secret structure. Angel plays his 'gotcha' card and it bounces off completely. The confidence of Skinner's response is funnier than any embarrassment could have been.

jokes.text: Angel's big revelation — 'Oh, but I am, Cousin Sissy' — lands as anticlimactic because Skinner is unfazed; the nickname 'Sissy' is already public knowledge
jokes.setup: Angel reveals he knows Skinner's intimate childhood nickname 'Cousin Sissy' as if it's a devastating secret.
jokes.punchline: Skinner calmly explains the nickname is widely known, completely deflating Angel's moment of triumph.
jokes.explanation: Classic detective-genre subversion: the 'gotcha' moment that isn't. Angel plays his trump card and Skinner doesn't blink. The structure is clean — setup expects revelation, punchline gives indifference. Skinner's total composure is funnier than any comeback he could have offered.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, Sissy Skinner.' / 'What a Gaylord.' / 'Thank you, Andrews.'
jokes.setup: Skinner is calmly explaining his ballet background and nickname aren't embarrassing
jokes.punchline: An off-screen officer loudly offers 'What a Gaylord' — a juvenile insult — and Skinner thanks him formally as if receiving a business compliment
jokes.explanation: The formal 'Thank you, Andrews' after the crude schoolyard insult is the joke — Skinner's unflappable poshness absorbs everything. The incongruity between register and content is very Edgar Wright.

jokes.text: 'Anything to energize my workforce.' — Skinner explaining he enjoys competition from other stores
jokes.setup: Skinner claims he welcomes competition from other shops rather than having motive to murder a rival
jokes.punchline: The corporate-speak 'energize my workforce' is hilariously banal as a defense against murder charges
jokes.explanation: Minor but effective — the contrast between management-speak and the murder accusation is funny, and Skinner's smooth delivery sells it. Not a standout but functional.

jokes.text: 'I myself host a life drawing class at the Village Hall. Tina here is a table dancer at Flappers.'
jokes.setup: Skinner is defending his employees having multiple jobs as normal
jokes.punchline: He offers himself (life drawing) and Tina (table dancer at a strip club called 'Flappers') as perfectly equivalent examples — the absurd pairing and the name 'Flappers' are the gags
jokes.explanation: The name 'Flappers' is a great gag — suitably British and euphemistic. The juxtaposition of 'life drawing class' (posh) and 'table dancer' (not posh) placed side-by-side as morally equivalent is funny, and Skinner's total equanimity sells it.

jokes.text: 'Well, you've got me there. I'd need something conclusive. Something that placed you at the scene of the crime. Perhaps a wound you sustained on a piece of broken glass this very evening.'
jokes.setup: Skinner challenges Angel to produce hard evidence
jokes.punchline: Angel pivots immediately to something very specific — a wound from broken glass — implying he already has this evidence, turning Skinner's confident challenge back on him
jokes.explanation: The shift from 'well, you've got me there' (apparent defeat) to the specific detail of the glass wound is a satisfying misdirection. The audience and Skinner both think Angel's out of ammo — the precision of 'this very evening' is a good beat.

jokes.text: 'How could I possibly be in several places at once?'
jokes.setup: Skinner is denying he could have committed multiple murders across different locations
jokes.punchline: The line is played straight but on rewatch is deeply ironic — the NWA is a conspiracy of many people; Skinner literally couldn't be everywhere, but collectively they were. Also echoes back as a callback at 76:28.
jokes.explanation: Seeds what becomes the film's central reveal. Good economy, works as a straight line now and pays off both as a callback and thematically when the conspiracy is revealed.

jokes.text: Skinner invites Angel to 'spool through' security footage — Angel does so, and presumably the footage shows Skinner at the store the whole evening.
jokes.setup: Angel is building a case placing Skinner at the murder scene
jokes.punchline: Skinner confidently hands over security footage that will exonerate him — the visual of Angel watching himself be defeated by a supermarket CCTV camera is the gag
jokes.explanation: A quiet visual defeat for Angel. Skinner's confidence in 'do feel free to spool through' is the punchline. Works as procedural comedy — the detective's grand theory crumbling against mundane evidence.

jokes.text: Angel tells Danny he might as well go enjoy the rest of his birthday — 'But it's been impounded as evidence. Well, I mean, maybe Dad will still let me water it, eh?'
jokes.setup: Angel bought Danny a Japanese Peace Lily for his birthday, which got caught up in the murder investigation
jokes.punchline: Danny's optimistic hope that his dad might let him water the impounded birthday plant is a touchingly absurd detail — the mundane domesticity of 'can I water it' against the murder investigation
jokes.explanation: A warm character beat that's also funny. Danny's innocent simplicity — hoping to water his birthday plant that's now murder evidence — is very specific to his character and earns genuine affection as well as a laugh.

jokes.text: 'Mr. Skinner, what you do with your land is of no concern of mine, so jog on.'
jokes.setup: Skinner delivers a sanctimonious speech about turning Leslie's land into a memorial garden
jokes.punchline: 'So jog on' — the British dismissal — delivered with perfect flat finality after a formal setup line, and also a callback to Skinner's fun-running
jokes.explanation: 'Jog on' works as a dismissal, as a British idiom, and as a callback to Skinner's fun-running escape. Three things at once in two syllables is excellent economy and high quotability.

jokes.text: Michael's single-word response 'Yarp.' to Skinner's instruction to escort Angel from the premises.
jokes.setup: Skinner gives a formal instruction
jokes.punchline: 'Yarp.' — Michael's signature affirmative, used as a formal response to a professional workplace instruction
jokes.explanation: Perfect character economy. One word, 100% character-specific, never gets old. The running gag is well-deployed here in a professional context.

jokes.text: 'She tripped and fell on her own shears.' — Repeated again to a new character expressing disbelief that Leslie is dead.
jokes.setup: Someone asks how Leslie died, in shock
jokes.punchline: Angel delivers the official cover story with flat deadpan — now on its third usage, it's become a running gag with the audience recognising it as the film's absurdist refrain
jokes.explanation: By this third use the line has become its own running gag and each repetition gets its own laugh from audience recognition. The comic mechanics of repetition are being executed precisely.

jokes.text: Beat after Angel delivers 'tripped and fell' line — 'Hey, that weren't me.'
jokes.setup: The flat delivery of the cover story creates a beat
jokes.punchline: An unprompted denial from a bystander who wasn't accused of anything — played as a non-sequitur reaction to the mention of a death near them
jokes.explanation: A quick throwaway that gets a mild laugh — the unprompted denial reads as either innocent nervousness or guilty deflection. Lightly funny, good economy.

jokes.text: 'Hey, look. Look, Mr. Treacher's got his big coat on again.'
jokes.setup: The scene has been dramatically tense — Angel humiliated, Danny concerned
jokes.punchline: Danny suddenly and genuinely notices and reports that Mr. Treacher has his big coat on — a completely irrelevant observation that reveals Danny's simple, easily-distracted nature
jokes.explanation: A deceptively brilliant character beat. After a tense scene, Danny's immediate pivot to noticing a coat is both hilarious and deeply character-specific. It's funny because it's completely sincere — Danny isn't deflecting; he genuinely finds this worth reporting. Earns 8 for exceptional character integration and perfect tonal shift.

jokes.text: 'You want anything from the shop?' / 'Cornetto.'
jokes.setup: In the middle of a murder investigation crisis, Danny offers to get something from the shop
jokes.punchline: Angel's immediate flat 'Cornetto' — the ice cream brand that runs as a motif through the Cornetto trilogy — delivered without hesitation mid-crisis
jokes.explanation: A beloved running gag that earns a big reaction from fans of the trilogy. The timing — Angel answering with 'Cornetto' as if it's a completely normal situation — is impeccable. High quotability and strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: 'No luck catching them killers, then?' / 'It's just the one killer, actually.'
jokes.setup: A casual bystander offers the village's breezy view of the murders
jokes.punchline: Angel's pedantic correction — 'it's just the one killer, actually' — is both a character moment (his precision) and ironic (later revealed to be many killers)
jokes.explanation: A multi-layered joke. On first viewing: funny because Angel corrects a casual bystander's grammar of murder. On rewatch: Angel is specifically wrong — it IS multiple killers. The pedantic correction being incorrect is an extra irony. 'Actually' is perfect economy. Earns 8+ for the structural intelligence.

jokes.text: 'What's the matter? You got brain-freeze?' / 'No, I got brainwave.'
jokes.setup: Danny sees Angel pause mid-Cornetto and assumes he has brain-freeze
jokes.punchline: Angel corrects 'brain-freeze' to 'brainwave' — a quick wordplay pivot that's also a plot beat (Angel realises the killer is plural)
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully tight piece of writing — the pun does triple duty: it's funny, it's character-specific to Angel's precision with words, and it's a plot pivot. 'Brainwave' as the correction to 'brain-freeze' is immediately quotable and the comedic timing of eating an ice cream while having a murder revelation is perfect.

jokes.text: Frank compares Angel's situation to that of 'Sergeant Popwell' — 'It was exactly the same thing.'
jokes.setup: Frank is sympathetically telling Angel he's seen detectives get 'driven round the bend' before
jokes.punchline: On rewatch, the comparison to Sergeant Popwell — who presumably met a bad end after getting too close to the truth — is terrifyingly ironic and darkly funny
jokes.explanation: Classic Edgar Wright foreshadowing played as reassurance. The dark subtext — Popwell was probably murdered by the NWA — is entirely in the audience's inference on rewatch. Frank's warmth while condemning Angel is excellent dramatic irony.

jokes.text: Michael's exchange with the conspirators: 'Yarp.' / 'He's not gonna get back up again?' / 'Narp!'
jokes.setup: Skinner asks if Angel has been 'taken care of'
jokes.punchline: Michael responds to both affirmative and negative questions about murder using his signature 'Yarp'/'Narp' — his monosyllabic quirk applied to confirming an assassination
jokes.explanation: The best use of the Yarp/Narp running gag in the film. The gag's charm was always its infantile simplicity — applying it to confirming an execution attempt is a perfect dark escalation. The addition of 'Narp!' (negating the 'get back up again' question) adds the extra beat that makes this land as a complete comedic exchange. Earns 8.5 — it's the running gag at peak deployment.

jokes.text: 'Frank, this shit just got real.'
jokes.setup: Angel is on the phone after narrowly escaping an assassination attempt
jokes.punchline: 'This shit just got real' is a clichéd action-movie catchphrase delivered by Angel — the ultimate straight-laced, professional police officer — which is both a genre parody and his first visible crack into action-hero mode
jokes.explanation: Angel adopting action-movie speak ('shit just got real') is the moment the film signals its shift from procedural parody to action-movie parody. Character-specific because it's completely out of his register — this precise man using this cliché marks a character turning point. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'Oh, my God. What happened to your Peace Lily?'
jokes.setup: Angel has just survived an assassination attempt and is covered in debris
jokes.punchline: Danny's first concern is for the Peace Lily birthday present, not for Angel's safety — perfect character-specific priorities
jokes.explanation: A supremely character-specific beat. Danny asking about the plant rather than Angel is both funny and reveals something true about him — his priorities are sweet, innocent, and absurd. The Peace Lily has been elevated to a beloved running detail by this point.

jokes.text: During Angel's montage of recalled dialogue, Skinner's line 'How could I possibly be in several places at once?' plays back.
jokes.setup: Angel is replaying conversations in his head as the penny drops that there are multiple killers
jokes.punchline: Skinner's earlier self-defense line now becomes the clue that cracks the case — the alibi proves the conspiracy
jokes.explanation: The structural elegance here earns 8+. Skinner's throwaway defense line becomes the exact mechanism that cracks the case. The audience doesn't get the joke until this moment — the earlier line retroactively becomes the setup. This is sophisticated long-form comedy construction.

jokes.text: NWA meeting opens with Janet Barker announcing the names of her new twin boys ('Roger and Martin') and their christening invitation — delivered as mundane community news before a murder conspiracy meeting.
jokes.setup: The NWA has just confirmed they've sent someone to kill Sergeant Angel
jokes.punchline: Before getting to murder business, they deal with christening logistics — 'a week on Saturday and we're all invited' — the banal neighbourhood warmth sitting alongside homicidal conspiracy
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best tonal jokes. The NWA operates exactly like a Parish Council — the christening announcement could belong to any village meeting. The juxtaposition of domestic warmth ('we're all invited') with the murder conspiracy they're conducting is very effective dark comedy. Earns 8+ for structural elegance and the depth of the film's satirical vision.

jokes.text: 'You'll all be delighted to hear that the tenacious Sergeant Angel has been taken care of. Joyce will discover the Sergeant lying on the wet floor of his bathroom, having slipped and tragically broken his neck.'
jokes.setup: The NWA announces Angel has been neutralized
jokes.punchline: The murder has already been given its official 'accident' cover story — presented at the meeting in advance, like scheduling. The word 'tragically' is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: Pre-preparing the 'tragic accident' cover story and presenting it to the meeting is terrific dark comedy. 'Having slipped and tragically broken his neck' delivered as event planning is excellent. The word 'tenacious' is also funny — it's a compliment embedded in a murder announcement.

jokes.text: 'Joyce will discover the Sergeant lying on the wet floor of his bathroom, having slipped and tragically broken his neck.'
jokes.setup: Frank is laying out the cover story for Angel's planned death.
jokes.punchline: The staged accident — the same method used for all the murders — is now being planned for Angel in the same meeting-minutes tone. The pattern of 'accidents' completing its full circle. 'Tragically' is funny.
jokes.explanation: Frank planning Angel's death the same way all the others were staged — with the same banal language — is the dark comedy escalation of the meeting sequence. 'Tragically' applied to a murder he's planning is very funny. The callback to the murder pattern gives it accumulated weight.

jokes.text: 'Oh, I beg to differ, Mr. Weaver. / Well, well, well, I see we have visitors.' — Angel's dramatic entrance into the NWA meeting
jokes.setup: An NWA member asserts that nothing now stands in their way.
jokes.punchline: Angel appears — having apparently tracked them to the castle — with a theatrically timed 'Oh, I beg to differ.' The genre satisfaction of the hero's entrance played for a laugh.
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, I beg to differ' is polite to a fault — Angel crashing a murder meeting with the manners of someone disagreeing at a committee meeting. The British understatement of the heroic entrance is very Edgar Wright.

jokes.text: NWA members chanting 'The greater good' in unison, repeatedly.
jokes.setup: Frank justifies the murders: 'It's all about the greater good'
jokes.punchline: The assembled conspirators chant 'The greater good' in creepy unison — the cult-like communal response to every justification
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most iconic and quotable moments. The chant reveals the NWA's true nature — a cult with the aesthetic of a Parish Council. The repetition escalates perfectly, each echo more absurd and menacing. 'THE GREATER GOOD' becomes the film's thesis delivered as punchline. Near-perfect scores across all dimensions.

jokes.text: 'Blower's fate was simply the result of his being an appalling actor.' / 'Quite appalling.' / 'You murdered him for that?' / 'Well, he murdered Bill Shakespeare.'
jokes.setup: Angel is demanding explanations for each murder
jokes.punchline: Martin Blower was murdered for being a bad actor. Skinner's justification — 'he murdered Bill Shakespeare' — is both a pun (murder as metaphor for bad performance) and a literal statement from a murderer
jokes.explanation: A legitimately great joke. 'He murdered Bill Shakespeare' is a double-meaning gem — Skinner, an actual murderer, using 'murdered' as theatrical slang while justifying an actual murder is a wordplay-structural triumph. The escalation of revealing the trivial reasons for each murder begins here and compounds brilliantly.

jokes.text: 'The Dramatic Society is an important feather in our cap. Couldn't let Blower jeopardize that. Not when we had two semi-professionals waiting in the wings.' / 'Let's not forget that Greg was an extra in Straw Dogs. And Sheree played a cadaver in Prime Suspect.'
jokes.setup: The NWA is explaining why murder was justified to protect the Dramatic Society
jokes.punchline: The 'semi-professionals' are defined as an extra in Straw Dogs and a cadaver in Prime Suspect — this is the talent they committed murder to elevate
jokes.explanation: The specific credits — extra in Straw Dogs, cadaver in Prime Suspect — are perfectly chosen. The word 'cadaver' is especially funny (a speaking role for a corpse). 'Yes, I know!' from Angel caps it perfectly. The gap between the crime (murder) and the motivation (bad amateur dramatics) achieves the comedic ideal.

jokes.text: 'Well, he murdered Bill Shakespeare. / What? / The Dramatic Society is an important feather in our cap. Couldn't let Blower jeopardize that.'
jokes.setup: Frank doubles down: murder was justified because Blower 'murdered' Shakespeare.
jokes.punchline: The complete earnestness with which the NWA defends the Dramatic Society's reputation as a reason to commit actual murder is both funny and a perfect character revelation. 'An important feather in our cap' as murder justification.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'he murdered Bill Shakespeare' — using 'murdered' figuratively in a conversation about literal murder — is a sharp piece of wordplay embedded in a dark revelation. The NWA's priorities (village reputation > human life) is the film's central comic idea and this is its clearest statement.

jokes.text: 'And so Eve deserved to die too?' / 'Well, she did have a very annoying laugh.' / 'Annoying.'
jokes.setup: The catalogue of murder justifications is escalating in triviality
jokes.punchline: Eve Draper was murdered for having an annoying laugh — the NWA chorus's confirmatory 'Annoying' is the kicker
jokes.explanation: Part of the escalating catalogue of trivial murder motivations. 'Annoying laugh' is the most recognisably relatable motivation yet, which makes it funnier and darker. The choral echo 'Annoying.' from the assembled murderers is superb — they're all nodding along to validating a murder for an annoying laugh.

jokes.text: 'And, and George Merchant?' / 'He had an awful house.' / 'Awful.'
jokes.setup: The catalogue continues — each justification more trivial than the last
jokes.punchline: George Merchant was murdered because he had an ugly house. The choral 'Awful.' is the echo.
jokes.explanation: If anything, 'He had an awful house' is funnier than 'annoying laugh' because it's purely aesthetic. The escalation is working perfectly — each revelation more absurdly petty. 'Awful.' as the congregational echo is pitch-perfect.

jokes.text: 'Tim Messenger's tenure as editor of the Sandford Citizen has been unbearable. Our once great paper had become riddled with tabloid journalism. Not to mention persistent errors.' / 'He listed her age as 55.' / 'When, actually, I'm 53.' / 'Fifty-three.'
jokes.setup: Tim Messenger was murdered for journalistic crimes against the village paper
jokes.punchline: The final, specific grievance is that he printed a woman's wrong age — she's 53, not 55 — and the communal chorus echoes 'Fifty-three' as if this is a capital offence
jokes.explanation: The best entry in the catalogue. After tabloid journalism (vaguely legitimate complaint), the specific outrage is a woman's age printed two years too old — and the whole NWA solemnly intoning 'Fifty-three.' seals it. The structure is superb: build a seemingly rational complaint, then reveal its true absurd crux. Earns near-9 for how perfectly this punctures the NWA's self-seriousness.

jokes.text: 'We couldn't have her sharing her green fingers with anybody else. Not least those heathens at Buford Abbey. If we can't have her, no one can.'
jokes.setup: Leslie Tiller was planning to move away and share her horticultural skills
jokes.punchline: 'If we can't have her, no one can' — a possessive murder justification that sounds like a jealous lover, applied to a gardener moving villages
