jokes.explanation: 'If we can't have her, no one can' applied to a gardener is both funny and revealing — the NWA's possessiveness over the village has curdled into genuine horror. The phrase 'heathens at Buford Abbey' is also funny — treating neighbouring villages as mortal enemies over flower-growing.

jokes.text: 'Before you could say, "Gypsy scum," we were knee-deep in dog muck, thieving kids and crusty jugglers.'
jokes.setup: Frank is delivering his tragic backstory about losing the Village of the Year contest to travellers
jokes.punchline: 'Crusty jugglers' — the specificity and absurdity of the phrase, landing after 'dog muck' and 'thieving kids', is so unexpected it's the punchline
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most quotable lines. 'Crusty jugglers' is an inspired piece of original comedy writing — specific, visual, British, and utterly absurd as the culmination of a list of traveller grievances. The phrase is unexpected enough to cause a genuine laugh while being completely within register for a bigoted Village stalwart. Earns 8.8 craft — only held back from 9+ because it's essentially a pure wordplay/list joke rather than a structurally complex construction.

jokes.text: 'Crusty jugglers.' — repeated by Angel in flat echo
jokes.setup: Frank delivers 'crusty jugglers' in his speech
jokes.punchline: Angel's flat repetition — processing what he just heard — is the reaction beat. His stunned echo is funnier than any snarky comment.
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'crusty jugglers' in Angel's completely flat register adds an extra beat to the original joke. It signals that Angel (and the audience) cannot quite believe what they've heard.

jokes.text: 'She drove her Datsun Cherry into Sandford Gorge.'
jokes.setup: Frank is delivering his tragic origin story about his wife's death — an emotional monologue about losing Sandford's Village of the Year title
jokes.punchline: The car model 'Datsun Cherry' is an absurdly specific, undignified detail for a suicide that Frank clearly finds important to include in his sincere tragic speech
jokes.explanation: A dark comedy beat in an otherwise emotionally sincere speech. The 'Datsun Cherry' is so mundane and specific — it's funny because it's the kind of detail only someone sincerely telling a story would include, and because a Datsun Cherry is an inherently undignified vehicle for a dramatic suicide.

jokes.text: 'And whatever the cost, we would make Sandford great again.'
jokes.setup: Frank is delivering his heartfelt resolve to restore Sandford's glory
jokes.punchline: 'Make Sandford great again' — either a prescient joke in 2007 or a deliberate satire of nationalist-populist rhetoric applied to a village competition
jokes.explanation: In 2007 this was a sharp satire of small-minded nationalist rhetoric applied to village politics; in the post-2016 world it has become even funnier and more pointed. The rewatch bonus accounts for how the line has aged. The satirical precision of applying 'great again' rhetoric to a Best Village competition is genuine comic intelligence.

jokes.text: 'Are you saying this is all about winning the Best Village Award?' / 'This is the best village, Nicholas.'
jokes.setup: Angel has just discovered the entire murder conspiracy's motivation
jokes.punchline: Frank's completely sincere, non-defensive 'This is the best village, Nicholas' — as if that explains everything — is the punchline. He's not embarrassed; he's proud.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of the ultimate motivation — a Best Village competition — lands as the film's central satirical punchline. Frank's pride rather than shame in answering 'This is the best village' is the perfect character beat. He means it completely. The gap between crime (serial murder) and motive (village award) is maximized here.

jokes.text: 'Back off! Back off! Or I swear to God, you'll be explaining how Danny tripped over and accidentally cut off his own head.'
jokes.setup: Angel is using Danny as a hostage/shield against the NWA
jokes.punchline: He threatens the NWA using the exact language of their own cover stories — 'tripped over and accidentally cut off his own head' — weaponizing their own absurd phrasing
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best jokes. Angel uses the NWA's own 'accident' language — escalating from 'tripped on shears' to 'accidentally cut off his own head' — as his threat. It's funny, structurally brilliant, character-perfect (he's adopted their logic), and extremely quotable. The absurdist specificity of 'cut off his own head' is superb. This is the best joke in the reel and one of the film's finest.

jokes.text: During Angel's escape/montage sequence, dialogue fragments repeat: 'Gypsy scum. Travelers. / Thieving kids. Dog muck. / Crusty jugglers.'
jokes.setup: Angel is piecing together the conspiracy from recalled fragments
jokes.punchline: 'Crusty jugglers' returns in the montage — its third repetition in this reel, now elevated to mantra-level absurdity
jokes.explanation: By its third appearance, 'crusty jugglers' has become a comedic refrain. The repetition in a montage context amplifies its absurdity — it's the punchline that keeps giving.

jokes.text: 'This is murder!' / 'It's not, it's ketchup.'
jokes.setup: Danny accuses Angel of 'murder'
jokes.punchline: Angel assumes he means the fake blood/ketchup covering him, and misses the point — a classic cross-purposes exchange
jokes.explanation: A classic misdirection: Danny means the murders of the NWA's victims; Angel deflects to the literal ketchup — accidentally inverting the conversation. Perfect economy and a great comedic misunderstanding that also advances character (Angel desperately trying to redirect).

jokes.text: 'I thought it was about rapping people on the knuckles and sending them on their way.'
jokes.setup: Danny is revealed to have known his dad ran a 'special club' but had a benign interpretation of what it was
jokes.punchline: His innocent understanding of the NWA — 'rapping people on the knuckles' — against the reality of a serial murder conspiracy is perfect character comedy
jokes.explanation: One of Danny's finest moments. 'Rapping people on the knuckles and sending them on their way' as his mental image of the NWA is absolutely character-perfect — it's exactly what an innocent, slightly simple, action-movie-loving kid would imagine a secret village council gets up to. High character integration score justified.

jokes.text: 'There are skeletons back there!' / 'I don't know nothing about no skelingtons.'
jokes.setup: Angel has found actual skeletons of previous victims
jokes.punchline: Danny's denial uses the childlike mispronunciation 'skelingtons' — both funny as a word and revealing that Danny is essentially a large child
jokes.explanation: 'Skelingtons' is an inspired malapropism. The double negative ('I don't know nothing') plus the childish mispronunciation plus the gravity of the situation (actual murder victims' remains) creates a perfect comedic incongruity. Highly quotable and extremely character-specific.

jokes.text: 'He's appointed himself judge, jury and executioner.' / 'He's not Judge Judy and executioner.'
jokes.setup: Angel delivers the serious accusation 'judge, jury and executioner'
jokes.punchline: Danny mishears/misremembers it as 'Judge Judy and executioner' — conflating the legal idiom with the American daytime TV judge
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the reel by a narrow margin from #47. 'Judge Judy and executioner' is a legitimately classic comedy line — it works as a malapropism, as a character beat revealing Danny watches daytime TV, as a wordplay joke (the sounds align perfectly), and as a tonal rupture. It's immediate, completely unexpected, and absolutely quotable. The craft scores reflect near-perfection in structure and character integration. This is the calibre of the 8.0 anchor and exceeds it.

jokes.text: 'I can come back, and I can bring the blue fury of the Metropolitan Police Service with me.'
jokes.setup: Angel is trying to convince Danny to let him go deal with the conspiracy
jokes.punchline: 'The blue fury of the Metropolitan Police Service' — Angel's bureaucratic action-hero speak, parodying tough-cop threats with hilariously institutional language
jokes.explanation: 'The blue fury of the Metropolitan Police Service' is funny because 'fury' is action-movie language while 'Metropolitan Police Service' is bureaucratic — the incongruity is characteristically Angel. It also parodies the action-hero threat scene.

jokes.text: 'They'll make it disappear. Who are they gonna believe? My dad, or a loony London police officer.'
jokes.setup: Danny is trying to convince Angel to give up and return to London
jokes.punchline: 'Loony London police officer' — Danny affectionately calling Angel crazy using the village's own vocabulary, which is rich given the village just tried to have Angel killed
jokes.explanation: A solid beat — Danny's use of 'loony' echoes all the dismissals of Angel from earlier in the film, now delivered by his best friend. The irony is good; the execution is functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: 'Forget it, Nicholas. It's Sandford.'
jokes.setup: Angel insists he can bring justice to the village
jokes.punchline: 'Forget it, Nicholas. It's Sandford' — a direct parody of 'Forget it, Jake. It's Chinatown' from Roman Polanski's Chinatown (1974), Danny's cinematic knowledge finally deployed
jokes.explanation: A magnificent piece of construction. The film has spent its runtime establishing Danny's obsession with films and Angel's professional rigidity. This line does everything: it's a perfect Chinatown parody, it's delivered by the character who would know the reference (Danny), and it crystallises the village's closed-off nature through a cinematic lens. The specificity ('Sandford' replacing 'Chinatown') earns maximum economy score. Near-perfect on craft — this is what a 9 looks like.

jokes.text: Long silent scene of Angel sitting alone in a pub/hotel. 'This is something I have to do myself.' — delivered after long pause.
jokes.setup: Angel appears to be giving up — sitting alone, apparently despairing, the barman asking if there's anything he can do
jokes.punchline: 'This is something I have to do myself' — a classic action-movie lone-hero beat, played dead straight, parodying the genre while also being genuinely sincere
jokes.explanation: A genre parody beat — the action hero's 'I work alone' moment — delivered with enough sincerity that it works both as parody and as genuine character resolve. Functional, not outstanding.

jokes.text: 'Another beautiful day in God's country.'
jokes.setup: Angel is about to ride back into the village to confront a murderous conspiracy
jokes.punchline: A completely oblivious villager cheerfully greets the morning — the idyllic village routine continuing entirely undisturbed despite the multiple murders and conspiracy
jokes.explanation: A quiet irony beat — 'God's country' applied to a village full of murderers. Functional tonal contrast but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Angel's return to the village — the 'Danny?' moment followed by Angel finding Danny's police uniform laid out for him.
jokes.setup: Angel seems to be returning alone
jokes.punchline: Danny has laid out Angel's full police uniform (and presumably his own) in preparation — the visual of the neatly presented kit signals Danny is in, without a word spoken. 'It's...' 'Angel.' caps it.
jokes.explanation: A visual gag with strong emotional and comedic payoff. Danny's wordless preparation of the uniforms is the sweetest possible way for him to rejoin — and 'Angel.' as the final word (Danny identifying the name on the kit?) lands with quiet satisfaction. The visuals do the work.

jokes.text: 'Oh, Sergeant Angel? Someone from London called for you.' [Angel rides back into village on a horse]
jokes.setup: Angel makes his dramatic return to Sandford, riding a horse into the police station
jokes.punchline: The desk officer's response to this is not the awe or shock it deserves — just 'Oh, Sergeant Angel? Someone from London called for you' — the bureaucratic normality against the cinematic drama
jokes.explanation: Classic Edgar Wright juxtaposition — the most cinematic entrance possible (a policeman on a horse) met with the most mundane possible response ('someone called for you'). The officer's total incuriosity about the horse is the joke. 'I'll tell them you'll ring them back' extends it perfectly.

jokes.text: 'Well, that's funny.' / 'What's that?' / 'I didn't know we had a mounted division.' / 'Nobody tells me nothing.'
jokes.setup: Angel rides a horse into the village/station for his dramatic return
jokes.punchline: Two officers react to the horse not with amazement but with mild workplace grievance — the 'mounted division' they weren't informed about. 'Nobody tells me nothing' is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: Superb deadpan. 'I didn't know we had a mounted division' recontextualizes a dramatic cinematic moment as a bureaucratic communication failure. 'Nobody tells me nothing' is a perfect cap — the man's grievance is entirely administrative. This is the best application of the film's bureaucratic vs. cinematic comedy register in this reel.

jokes.text: 'Wanna do something useful?' — Angel recruiting the horse for the confrontation
jokes.setup: Angel is about to ride into battle against the village conspiracy
jokes.punchline: He asks the horse if it wants to 'do something useful' — treating the animal as a willing colleague in the action-movie mode
jokes.explanation: Light but effective. The genre convention of recruiting an ally — here applied to a horse — is a small action-movie parody beat that works with Angel's escalating action-hero mode.

jokes.text: 'Wanna do something useful?' — Angel recruiting someone (implied: a swan) or a local for the fight
jokes.setup: Angel needs assistance for his one-man assault.
jokes.punchline: Given the film's earlier running gag about the aggressive swan, 'Wanna do something useful?' directed at an animal (or unlikely local) is a callback to the swan/animal gag and positions it as action-movie recruit.
jokes.explanation: The phrasing 'wanna do something useful' as a team-up offer to what is presumably an animal (given the gap before the next dialogue) is good economy. The callback to the swan gives it accumulated funny.

jokes.text: 'Annette, that Sergeant Angel's back. Check out his horse.' / 'Roger that!'
jokes.setup: Angel rides dramatically into town on a horse
jokes.punchline: Officers casually radio each other about the horse using police radio protocol — 'Roger that!' — treating the sight of a cop on a horse as just another thing to report in
jokes.explanation: Another beat on the 'everyone is weirdly unbothered by the horse' theme — this time via police radio. 'Check out his horse' / 'Roger that' is funny because it has the shape of urgent police communication applied to horse-watching. Slight diminishing returns from joke 60 but still lands.

jokes.text: 'Morning.' — Angel's single-word greeting as he rides in full uniform on a horse into the village square.
jokes.setup: The film has built to Angel's cinematic showdown moment — full uniform, horse, against the entire village
jokes.punchline: 'Morning.' — the most English, mundane greeting possible as the punchline to a dramatic action-movie entrance. The understatement is total.
jokes.explanation: One of the great single-word punchlines in British comedy cinema. The entire reel — the horse, the uniform, the dramatic ride-in, the villagers watching — has built to this. And the punchline is 'Morning.' It's perfectly in character (Angel is unfailingly polite and professional), it's the ultimate anti-climactic-climax, and it encapsulates everything the film has been doing with English understatement vs. American action-movie grandeur. This earns a 9+ on craft — maximum economy, maximum character integration, maximum structural payoff.

jokes.text: Fascist!
jokes.setup: An intense, escalating action-sequence confrontation in a quaint English village — the stakes are life and death
jokes.punchline: The best insult a murderous posh villain can muster is 'Fascist!' — a word absurdly small for the situation
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the incongruity: a murderous NWA conspirator, in the middle of a pitched battle, pulls out the most milquetoast political insult imaginable. The single-word economy is perfect — no explanation needed.

jokes.text: Hag!
jokes.setup: 'Fascist!' is hurled as an insult mid-battle; the audience expects a more action-hero retort from Nicholas
jokes.punchline: Nicholas fires back with 'Hag!' — an equally absurd, almost Victorian insult, perfectly matching the register
jokes.explanation: The joke builds on the previous 'Fascist!' beat with perfect comic escalation. Wright sets up a call-and-response insult exchange that escalates in absurdity precisely because it deflates. 'Hag!' is funnier than 'Fascist!' because it's even more unexpected from the hyper-competent supercop. The pairing makes both jokes stronger. This is a tight, well-structured two-beat gag.

jokes.text: "Oh, fuck off, Grasshopper."
jokes.setup: The Reverend makes a solemn appeal to Nicholas as "a man of peace," and Nicholas responds with a genuinely sincere, almost poetic statement about knowing right from wrong — building toward what sounds like a noble speech moment
jokes.punchline: He punctures his own earnestness immediately with "Oh, fuck off, Grasshopper" — delivered at the Reverend mid-action
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the reel. It earns its high scores on multiple axes: (1) Structure is near-perfect — the earnest setup of the speech makes the deflation land harder; (2) Character integration is exceptional — only Nicholas, who is simultaneously principled and action-movie terse, could deliver sincerity and then immediately drop a casually contemptuous F-bomb; (3) The word 'Grasshopper' does enormous work — it's a callback to their mentor/pupil dynamic and reframes it mockingly in one word; (4) Economy is total — five words do the job of a paragraph. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor benchmark and exceeds it slightly due to the callback layering.

jokes.text: Dr. Hatcher: "I brought you into this world, I think it's rather fitting I should be the one to take you out of it."
jokes.setup: Dr. Hatcher, Danny's father figure and village doctor, confronts Nicholas and Danny with a gun
jokes.punchline: He delivers the classic villain monologue line — "I brought you into this world" — but it's the DOCTOR saying it, which makes it both literally true (he delivered Danny as a baby) and darkly absurd
jokes.explanation: The joke exploits a double meaning that most action-villain speeches don't have available: a doctor saying 'I brought you into this world' is literally accurate. The character specificity elevates what would otherwise be a generic villain line into something that actually earns its dark laugh.

jokes.text: "You're a doctor, deal with it." / "Yeah, motherfucker."
jokes.setup: Dr. Hatcher has been defeated/incapacitated; he's a doctor
jokes.punchline: Nicholas curtly tells the wounded villain to self-treat ("You're a doctor, deal with it"), then Danny adds an incongruous hip-hop tough-guy affirmation: "Yeah, motherfucker"
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: Nicholas's line is dry, logical, and perfectly in character — he doesn't do banter, he just processes the situation efficiently. Danny's "Yeah, motherfucker" is the action-movie hype-man addition that is completely incongruous from this gentle, movie-obsessed village constable. The contrast between who Danny is and what he says is rich character comedy.

jokes.text: Pub?
jokes.setup: Nicholas and Danny have just survived an intense life-or-death confrontation; Danny asks 'What you thinking?'
jokes.punchline: Nicholas's one-word answer — 'Pub?' — subverts any expectation of a heroic next-move declaration with the most mundane English suggestion possible
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word does everything. After intense action, 'Pub?' is the most English possible deflation. It's also a callback to the film's running affection for the local pub as the heart of the village. The question mark in the delivery implies Nicholas is genuinely asking, like they're deciding where to have lunch. Near-perfect joke economy; high quotability.

jokes.text: "This is ridiculous." / "No, it's not, Dad. It's very unridiculous."
jokes.setup: Frank dismisses the conspiracy reveal as ridiculous
jokes.punchline: Danny earnestly counters with "very unridiculous" — a malapropism/neologism that reveals Danny's dim but wholehearted sincerity
jokes.explanation: "Unridiculous" is a perfect Danny word — he wants to agree with Nicholas passionately but doesn't have the vocabulary, so he invents one. It's endearing and funny simultaneously. The doubling down ("It's very unridiculous") is what seals it. Strong character integration: this could only come from Danny.

jokes.text: Danny: "Mum is dead, Dad. For the first time in my life, you know, I'm glad. If she could see what you've become, I think she'd probably kill herself all over again."
jokes.setup: Frank tries to silence Danny by invoking his dead mother: "Think of your mother."
jokes.punchline: Danny turns the manipulation back with brutal dark logic: Mum is dead, he's glad she can't see this, and she'd "kill herself all over again" — implying she died by suicide, used here as a devastating rhetorical weapon by someone who is usually gentle
jokes.explanation: This is dark comedy that works because Danny — who is fundamentally good-natured and not particularly articulate — lands on the most devastating possible response through his own emotional rawness rather than wit. The "all over again" implication is genuinely shocking and very funny precisely because it comes from Danny. The structure of flipping the manipulation device back on the manipulator is elegant.

jokes.text: "Sorry, I am completely lost."
jokes.setup: Nicholas has delivered a rapid-fire exposition dump about the NWA conspiracy and 20 years of village murders
jokes.punchline: Doris, a police officer who has been standing there the whole time, admits she has no idea what's happening — a perfect deflation of the dramatic monologue
jokes.explanation: Functional audience-surrogate comedy — Doris voices what a confused bystander would feel. It deflates the earnest exposition nicely. Not exceptional, but well-placed and in character.

jokes.text: Radio relay: "I reckon he's got something there." / "He says, 'He reckons you got something there.'" / "I know."
jokes.setup: An officer communicates support for Nicholas via radio, but it has to be relayed through a third party
jokes.punchline: The relay is performed completely literally — word for word — and Nicholas acknowledges it with a flat "I know," making the unnecessary relay even more absurd
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the bureaucratic absurdity of relaying a simple statement through an intermediary during a tense standoff. Nicholas's unfazed "I know" treats it as perfectly normal, which is the deadpan cherry on top. Solid structural comedy.

jokes.text: Frank: "He isn't even from round here."
jokes.setup: Frank tries to discredit Nicholas's conspiracy expose to the assembled officers
jokes.punchline: His final argument — after all the murder revelations — is that Nicholas isn't a local. The pettiest, most parochial defense imaginable
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy: Frank has committed dozens of murders and his defense is local snobbery. It's also a sharp satirical point about parochialism as a tool of social control. Very economical, very specific to this world.

jokes.text: "You incompetent flatfoots!"
jokes.setup: Frank realizes he's losing the argument and his fellow officers are turning against him
jokes.punchline: He resorts to insulting the police he has commanded for years as "flatfoots" — an antiquated, pompous insult that reveals his contempt even as his control collapses
jokes.explanation: Decent character moment — Frank's pomposity is exposed as his authority crumbles. The word "flatfoots" is amusingly archaic. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: "Want anything from the shop?"
jokes.setup: In the middle of a dramatic police mobilization — officers receiving orders, preparing to go after the villain — one officer is left behind to guard
jokes.punchline: He casually asks if anyone wants anything from the shop, as if this is a normal errand run rather than the climax of a murder conspiracy
jokes.explanation: Classic Edgar Wright deadpan deflation — the mundane intrudes on the momentous. The officer's complete normalization of a crisis situation is funny and also a subtle joke about small-town policing. Very economical.

jokes.text: Nicholas's tactical briefing: "Go in through the front entrance, take the place aisle by aisle." / "Very good. What he said."
jokes.setup: Nicholas delivers a crisp military-style briefing for storming the supermarket. The officers listen attentively.
jokes.punchline: Simon Skinner — the supermarket manager turned villain — immediately co-opts the plan with "Very good. What he said," as if he's still managing the store
jokes.explanation: Skinner's managerial instinct — to defer to the competent person and endorse their plan — kicks in even when that person is arresting him. It's deeply in character, absurdly funny, and plays on the theme of Skinner being fundamentally a retail manager even as a murderous conspirator.

jokes.text: "My, my. Here come the fuzz."
jokes.setup: The police are arriving at Skinner's supermarket
jokes.punchline: Skinner narrates their arrival with a smirking "Here come the fuzz" — the film's own title, delivered by a villain watching cops approach his store
jokes.explanation: Light meta-reference — the villain uses the film's title as casual villain banter. It's self-aware without being winking or smug. Skinner's cool composure makes it land well.

jokes.text: "Don't worry, he knows what he's doing." (said as Nicholas goes in alone against an armed supermarket of conspirators)
jokes.setup: Nicholas goes in alone against a supermarket full of armed villains, against explicit advice
jokes.punchline: Danny reassures the other officers with complete confidence — "he knows what he's doing" — which is simultaneously true (Nicholas IS competent) and absurd given the situation
jokes.explanation: Functional comic reassurance beat — Danny's faith in Nicholas is endearing and slightly absurd. Not a standout but earns its place.

jokes.text: Nicholas to the trolley boy: "Is this what you really, really want?" / "Yarp." / "Suit yourself."
jokes.setup: Nicholas confronts the trolley boy (who has been a minor recurring threat) and gives him a final chance to stand down
jokes.punchline: "Yarp" — the trolley boy's monosyllabic catchphrase — confirms he wants to fight, and Nicholas responds with the most businesslike "Suit yourself" imaginable before presumably defeating him off-screen
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy and callback payoff. The trolley boy has been defined entirely by "Yarp" — so when Nicholas gives him a solemn, sincere out and receives "Yarp" (yes, I still want to fight), it's the character's entire arc in one word. Nicholas's "Suit yourself" is the action hero equivalent of a shrug — maximum cool, minimum words. This approaches the 8.0 anchor and arguably meets it. High quotability because "Yarp" has become genuinely beloved.

jokes.text: "How's Lurch?" / "He's in the freezer." / "Did you say, 'Cool off'?" / "No, I didn't say anything, actually." / "Shame."
jokes.setup: Danny asks about a defeated villain who's been put in the freezer. This is a direct parody of the action-movie one-liner tradition (characters say witty quips after defeating enemies)
jokes.punchline: Nicholas — unlike the Hollywood cops Danny idolizes — did NOT say a cool pun. Danny is disappointed. "Shame." The film consciously subverts the action-movie trope it's been celebrating
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the reel. It operates on three levels simultaneously: (1) It's a parody of action-movie one-liner culture; (2) It's a character moment — Nicholas is too professional and earnest to do banter, while Danny is so movie-obsessed he goes looking for the pun afterwards; (3) The structure is flawless — setup (asking if he said "cool off"), denial, and then Danny's deflated "Shame" which is both funny and oddly poignant about the gap between movies and reality. The "Shame" lands like a punchline AND a character beat. This is comparable to the 9.5 anchor in structural craft, though not quite in cultural impact.

jokes.text: Danny recaps what Nicholas missed: "There was a bit earlier on that you missed when I distracted him with the cuddly monkey. And then I said, 'Playtime's over,' and I hit him with the Peace Lily."
jokes.setup: Danny is excitedly telling Nicholas about his own combat achievements while they're in the middle of a gunfight
jokes.punchline: Danny HAS said a one-liner ("Playtime's over"), and he's so proud of it he recounts it in real-time. The weapons — a cuddly monkey and a Peace Lily — are gloriously incongruous with action-movie combat
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy. Danny has FULFILLED the one-liner fantasy — using the most un-action-movie weapons possible (a cuddly monkey, a Peace Lily) and delivering a pun so earnestly that he has to report it to Nicholas like a child reporting a good grade. The incongruity of the weapons is visually hilarious. Character integration is as high as it gets — no other character in cinema would fight with and narrate these choices.

jokes.text: "You're off the fucking chain!"
jokes.setup: Nicholas hears Danny's recap of fighting with a cuddly monkey and a Peace Lily
jokes.punchline: Nicholas — the hyper-competent, by-the-book officer — delivers a full action-movie hype response: "You're off the fucking chain!" This is NOT how Nicholas normally speaks
jokes.explanation: Nicholas has absorbed some of Danny's action-movie enthusiasm — him using this slang is a character evolution payoff as much as a joke. Works well in the sequence.

jokes.text: "What's the situation?" / "Two blokes and a fuckload of cutlery."
jokes.setup: Nicholas asks for a tactical situation report in the supermarket
jokes.punchline: "Two blokes and a fuckload of cutlery" — a crisp, profane, perfectly calibrated threat assessment that reduces the danger to its barest supermarket-aisle terms
jokes.explanation: "A fuckload of cutlery" is a great comedy phrase — it uses military/police sitrep language for a supermarket-aisle weapon inventory. The profanity is calibrated perfectly ("fuckload" is specific and funny, not gratuitous). Highly quotable. The structure of the sitrep format creating comic expectation before delivering a mundane-yet-absurd threat is well-executed.

jokes.text: "Nice one, Doris." / "Nothing like a bit of girl on girl."
jokes.setup: Doris has apparently just defeated a female opponent
jokes.punchline: Doris makes a self-satisfied double-entendre about "girl on girl" — delivered with complete casualness, turning her own combat into a bawdy comment
jokes.explanation: Functional bawdy joke, in character for Doris (the film's designated bawdy comedy relief). The double entendre is not especially inventive but it lands because of the timing and Doris's breezy delivery of it. Mid-tier.

jokes.text: Fruit attack!
jokes.setup: The supermarket fight continues; someone announces their attack
jokes.punchline: The 'attack' is literally fruit — produce thrown as weapons — and announcing it as 'Fruit attack!' is both a battle cry and a warning, in the most absurd possible framing
jokes.explanation: Pure absurdist comedy — the specificity of calling it 'Fruit attack!' with the same urgency as a live-fire announcement. Visual gag as well, since the audience sees produce being wielded as weapons.

jokes.text: "Don't go being a twat now." / "I wouldn't give you the satisfaction."
jokes.setup: Danny warns Nicholas not to do something reckless before they split up to pursue the villain
jokes.punchline: Nicholas's response — "I wouldn't give you the satisfaction" — is a perfect deadpan action-hero line that also reveals he's fully absorbed Danny's cinematic sensibility. It's also, incidentally, a correct use of the trope.
jokes.explanation: Good partner-comedy exchange. Nicholas has evolved — he delivers a proper action-movie line, but the specific choice of "I wouldn't give you the satisfaction" is perfectly calibrated: it's a comeback to an insult that isn't an insult, which makes it even better.

jokes.text: "How?" / "Skip."
jokes.setup: Officers need to get down from somewhere quickly during the chase
jokes.punchline: "Skip" — Nicholas proposes the most practical, undignified mode of descent as if it's a perfectly normal tactical option
jokes.explanation: One-word punchline with perfect economy. The physical comedy of police officers skipping presumably follows. The comedic value is in the word's unexpected mundanity as a tactical solution.

jokes.text: "Head them off?" / "Fuck, yeah."
jokes.setup: Nicholas and Danny coordinate on the chase
jokes.punchline: "Fuck, yeah" — Danny's enthusiastic, action-movie-junkie affirmation, delivered with maximum energy
jokes.explanation: Light character comedy — Danny's enthusiasm is always funny, but this is a thinner version of earlier, better beats. Functional.

jokes.text: Head them off? / Fuck, yeah.
jokes.setup: The two are coordinating action
jokes.punchline: 'Fuck, yeah' — Danny's enthusiastic, completely unbureaucratic agreement. The casualness and profanity from Danny is an expression of pure joy at doing action-movie stuff
jokes.explanation: Minor character beat — Danny's enthusiasm is consistent and endearing but this particular instance doesn't add much beyond his standard energy.

jokes.text: "I'll drive." / "Shotgun! Punch that shit!"
jokes.setup: They're getting into a police car to chase the villain
jokes.punchline: Danny calls "Shotgun!" and immediately follows with "Punch that shit!" — an action-movie command for the car stereo that sounds like a tactical order
jokes.explanation: "Punch that shit!" is a great Danny line — it conflates action-movie car chase music with an actual tactical command. The energy is infectious and it's a good callback payoff.

jokes.text: "Stay back! Or the ginger nut gets it!" (villain taking a child hostage)
jokes.setup: Skinner takes a child hostage in a desperate last move
jokes.punchline: His hostage threat is delivered with his usual retail-manager smoothness, but the specific descriptor — "ginger nut" — for the child is both darkly funny and reveals how casually contemptuous he is even in crisis
jokes.explanation: Skinner's casual cruelty and odd vocabulary make even his hostage threats feel like customer service interactions. "Ginger nut" is an amusingly specific, dismissive British insult applied to a child he's threatening. Solid character comedy.

jokes.text: "You did good, kid." / "Ta." / "What's your name?" / "Aaron A. Aaronson." / "Sorry?" / "Angel!"
jokes.setup: Nicholas gives a standard action-hero debrief to a young person who helped — "You did good, kid." The kid replies "Ta" (British for thanks), then Nicholas asks his name in a movie-cliché moment
jokes.punchline: "Aaron A. Aaronson" — a spectacularly alphabetically-first name that is aggressively absurd. Nicholas's "Sorry?" is the straight-man beat, then Danny shouts "Angel!" cutting off the awkward exchange
jokes.explanation: "Aaron A. Aaronson" is a brilliantly absurd name — it reads like someone who wanted to be first in every directory. The setup of the action-movie "what's your name, kid" moment makes the reveal funnier. "Ta" is also funny as the most un-cinematic response to "you did good." Well-structured sequence.

jokes.text: "I'm going to need some ice-cream."
jokes.setup: Danny has apparently been injured (shot or hurt) in the climactic confrontation
jokes.punchline: His response to injury is not stoic or dramatic — it's a request for ice-cream, delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: Perfect character moment. Danny is injured — which should be solemn — and his response is a child's comfort request. It works because it's completely authentic to who Danny is: soft, food-motivated, movie-loving. The callback to ice cream as his comfort item adds an emotional layer. Genuinely funny AND touching. Excellent character integration.

jokes.text: "Yeah, well, don't worry. There's plenty of ice-cream at the station. Isn't that right, Danny?"
jokes.setup: Danny asked for ice-cream after being injured
jokes.punchline: Nicholas — the hyper-professional supercop — knows exactly where the station ice-cream is and deploys this information instantly to calm his partner
jokes.explanation: Nicholas knowing the ice-cream situation at the station is an unexpected character reveal — it shows how fully he's adopted Sandford and Danny's world. The gentle way he uses it to manage the wounded Danny is both funny and warm. Good payoff.

jokes.text: "The figures have gone a little squiffy in your absence, it has to be said."
jokes.setup: Nicholas's London superiors have come to Sandford to persuade him to return; they frame the situation professionally
jokes.punchline: "Squiffy" — a comically British, whimsical understatement for what are presumably serious crime statistics, delivered by a police chief trying to sound authoritative
jokes.explanation: "Squiffy" is a funny word choice for a police briefing — the linguistic register clash between official police speak and this whimsical British colloquialism is the joke. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "Fuck's sake, Nick, this is gonna take ages." / "Yeah, it's gonna take all night." / "Well, good job we've got the manpower, Andy?"
jokes.setup: The officers face a mountain of post-incident paperwork
jokes.punchline: Nicholas sets up a "manpower" remark — clearly about to be corrected — which pays off immediately in the next line
jokes.explanation: The setup for the "manpower" joke. Functional structure comedy, nothing exceptional on its own.

jokes.text: Fuck's sake, Nick, this is gonna take ages. / Yeah, it's gonna take all night.
jokes.setup: The aftermath of the climax — the officers face a mountain of paperwork for all the crimes, deaths, and destruction
jokes.punchline: Even after the most extreme action-movie climax, the British police still face crushing bureaucratic paperwork — the film returns to its mundane institutional reality
jokes.explanation: Thematic callback to Nicholas's London origin as a hyper-bureaucratic officer — the idea that action-movie heroism still ends in British administrative tedium is a consistent joke throughout the film.

jokes.text: "Official vocab guidelines state that we say 'staffing,' not 'manpower,' 'cause 'manpower's' a bit sexist."
jokes.setup: Nicholas uses the word "manpower" in a casual context
jokes.punchline: Andy delivers a formal HR/policy correction about gender-neutral language — in a police station that has just resolved a mass-murder conspiracy, surrounded by chaos
jokes.explanation: The joke is about bureaucratic normality reasserting itself immediately after extraordinary events — the first order of business after defeating a murder cult is correct HR language. Andy's pedantry is in character and the timing (amid the chaos of the aftermath) is well-chosen.

jokes.text: "You don't mind a bit of manpower do you, Doris?" / "Oh, dirty bastard!" / "Andy! / You cheeky fucker!"
jokes.setup: Andy has just been corrected about "manpower" being sexist
jokes.punchline: He immediately makes a double-entendre with the same word directed at Doris — using the exact word he was just told not to, now with an explicitly sexual connotation. Doris and Nicholas both react with exasperated profanity.
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent: correction → immediate violation of correction in the worst possible way. The fact that Andy makes it sexual the moment he's told it's problematic is a perfect character beat for the most laddish officer. Doris and Nicholas's profanity reactions are funnier than any straight response would be.

jokes.text: "You know what you are? A bloody busybody!"
jokes.setup: Nicholas has just solved a 20-year murder conspiracy and saved the village from a psychopathic neighbourhood watch
jokes.punchline: Someone calls him a "bloody busybody" — the most passive-aggressive, neighbourhood-dispute insult, as if solving murders is just being nosy
jokes.explanation: "Busybody" recontextualizes Nicholas's heroism through the lens of small-town parochialism. It's a great satirical note — the village's reaction to being saved is mild resentment at the intrusion. Economical and character-world specific.

jokes.text: "No!" (cut to — clearly something absurd happens, possibly the model village or a pratfall, inferred from the horrified reaction)
jokes.setup: Post-climax wind-down; then something unexpected occurs
jokes.punchline: A horrified "No!" at something — likely a visual gag (the model village being destroyed, a final threat, or an absurd physical mishap). The horror in the reaction is disproportionate to whatever petty thing presumably caused it.
jokes.explanation: Hard to score this fully without visuals — from dialogue alone it's just a horrified reaction. Given the film's pattern, this is almost certainly a visual gag payoff. Scored conservatively based on what the transcript confirms.

jokes.text: Danny being injured/shot — "Oh, God." / "Hold on, Danny, just hold on. It's gonna be fine. Everything's gonna be fine." (earnest repetition undercut by the fact we've seen this play out in action movies)
jokes.setup: Danny is injured — Nicholas delivers the action-movie "hang on, it's gonna be fine" speech with total sincerity
jokes.punchline: Nicholas repeating "everything's gonna be fine" multiple times — played straight, but the meta-joke is that this is THE action movie injured-partner cliché, being performed by people who have discussed action movies all film
jokes.explanation: This scene functions simultaneously as genuine drama and parody — the tension is real, but savvy viewers will recognise it as the classic action movie partner-in-peril beat that Danny would have been able to predict. The comedy is bittersweet and subtle rather than laugh-out-loud.

jokes.text: "Chief, we've had a report of some hippy types messing with the recycling bins at the supermarket."
jokes.setup: The film is winding toward its ending — things are returning to normal in Sandford after the catastrophic events
jokes.punchline: Normal police business has resumed: the report coming in is about hippies at recycling bins — the most trivial, Sandford-village-specific "crime" imaginable, echoing the absurd non-crimes at the film's start
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural callback — the film opens with Nicholas being frustrated by trivial Sandford policing, and it closes with that same trivial policing resuming, now embraced rather than mocked. The specific details (hippies, recycling bins) are perfectly Sandford. Good structural comedy.

jokes.text: "Sergeant Butterman, little hand says it's time to rock and roll." / "Bring the noise."
jokes.setup: Nicholas and Danny are back at work, responding to the trivial Sandford call
jokes.punchline: Nicholas uses the action-movie language Danny has taught him all film — "little hand says it's time to rock and roll" / "Bring the noise" — to dispatch them to deal with hippies at a recycling bin. The epic deployed for the mundane.
jokes.explanation: The perfect ending beat. Nicholas has fully adopted Danny's action-movie vocabulary and uses it to dispatch them to the most un-action-movie crime possible. The structure is a beautiful closing circle: the entire film has been about Nicholas learning to embrace this world and Danny. The fact that Nicholas says this — the man who could barely discuss action movies in reel one — is the ultimate character payoff. "Bring the noise" from Danny confirms the partnership is complete. This is as good as the 8.0 anchor and arguably better for its structural elegance as a film-closing beat.
